subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEVELOPMENT OF SECONDARY MORTGAGE MARKET

speakeroldname: Hon. D. J. Walker (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEVELOPMENT OF SECONDARY MORTGAGE MARKET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house of certain actions being taken by the government to develop a secondary mortgage market in Canada and thus to increase the flow of private investment into housing and contribute to greater stability in the construction industry.
Since 1954 the National Housing Act has provided for the purchase and sale of insured mortgage loans. Activity in this field, however, has never been very substantial. The result has been that in periods of reduced private investment in N.H.A. mortgages very large amounts of government funds have had to be made available to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for direct lending purposes.
The first step necessary to encourage an active market is to ensure that there is an ample supply of existing mortgages available to interested buyers. Accordingly the government has instructed C.M.H.C. to offer for sale as soon as possible, at reasonably attractive yields to investors, mortgages now held in its portfolio as a result of the extensive direct lending operations it has undertaken since this government took office in 1957. The saleable component in the C.M.H.C. portfolio exceeds $750 million, and the corporation will make available for sale whatever portion is required to lay a firm basis for an active market.
90205-6-234J
The government is confident that the development of an active secondary mortgage market will create not only a more regular but actually a larger demand for N.H.A. mortgages. The ability to dispose of mortgages in the market should encourage approved lenders to undertake more lending. However, if a secondary mortgage market is to be developed and maintained it is apparent that there will have to be greater flexibility in the determination and setting of the maximum N.H.A. rate on new mortgages and this rate will have to be kept more closely in line with other long term interest rates. Accordingly the government proposes, under section 4 of the National Housing Act, a semi-annual review of the N.H.A. interest ceiling having in mind the long term yield on government bonds prevailing at that time.
It is anticipated that the market will develop in two ways; through the sale of blocks of mortgage loans by one institution to another or among pension funds and trusts, and through sales to a new type of company, some of which are already in existence, which would enable the small investor to participate in the mortgage market through purchase of its debentures or shares.
The prices at which N.H.A. insured mortgages are to be sold will depend. of course, upon many considerations, including the interest rate at which the mortgage was written, the life of the mortgage still to run and the condition of the capital market at the time of sale. It is quite apparent that a mortgage bearing 6 per cent interest will sell at a price less than one bearing 6f per cent interest. Let me make it perfectly clear, however, that the sale of mortgages by C.M.H.C. does not in any way affect the interests of borrowers, which are defined when the mortgage is issued and do not change when it is sold.
There remain several technical and procedural matters to be resolved. I was sure, however, that the house would want to know of this further significant step which the government proposes for the promotion of housing and the development of the Canadian capital market.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-72 is the last of the measures arising out of the supplementary budget of December 20 last awaiting enactment. It is in precisely the same form as the resolution which was reported back to the house by the committee of ways and means on March 2. That resolution, quite apart from the budget debate in December and January last, was debated in the committee of ways and means on February 1, 2, 3, 15 and 27, and on March 2. I trust, therefore, that the ground has been quite fully covered and it will not be necessary to traverse the same ground at length.
In the present debate we are concerned with the principle of the bill. May I define what I conceive to be the principle of the bill. The concept of "class or kind" goods in the Customs Tariff dates, in its present form, from the Fielding budget of 1907. The concept really made its first appearance in the Customs Tariff in 1873. The concept contemplates that there shall be different customs duty rates with respect to goods, depending upon whether those goods are of a class or kind made in Canada. If they are not of a class or kind made in Canada the Customs Tariff rate is lower. If they are of a class or kind made in Canada the customs duties are accordingly higher.
Not only does the rate of customs duty differ depending upon the determination of this question, but the application of dumping duty as well. We have had provision for dumping duties in our legislation since 1904, and it is open to the government to apply dumping duties only in the case of goods of a class or kind of goods made in Canada. The purpose of such legislation, undoubtedly and unblushingly, is protective; it certainly was in 1907 and has been ever since. It is intended to provide encouragement for the manufacture and production of goods in Canada. The expression appears in numerous items of the Customs Tariff, indeed 70 or more.
The interpretation and application of these terms in the Customs Tariff presented really no problem until the last decade, but in this last decade the course of decisions has been to erode the accepted meaning of these words and reduce the intended benefit to Canadian 90205-6-235
Customs Tariff
producers. Indeed, the course of decision in this decade has created some quite extraordinary results; one which engaged the attention of the committee of ways and means was the shovel case. This was the case of the import of a power shovel having a 2J-yard capacity. It was competitive with a 2-yard shovel which was made in Canada but, because the 2|

yard size had never been made in Canada, it was held that such machines were of a class or kind not made in Canada, regardless of the fact that the facilities existed in Canada for the manufacture of a 2J-yard shovel.
We are living in the era of GATT, and have for the past 14 years. We support GATT, and under GATT trade advantages in markets of different countries are a matter of bargaining and agreement. For reductions in the Canadian tariff in favour of imports from other countries we bargain, and often bargain hard, for a price: a price in the form of similar advantages extended to Canadian exporters in the markets of the foreign country or countries concerned. When, in the course of bargaining, common ground is reached in regard to the price to be paid, that is to say in terms of mutual exchanges of tariff advantages, then we enter into an agreement with such country or countries. We do not give advantages of this kind away for nothing in this era of GATT.
Under GATT rates of customs duties are bound. Never has the definition of "class or kind" been bound under any GATT agreement. Erosion of the meaning of the expression has, therefore, given advantage to other countries exporting to Canadian markets, advantages for which they never bargained and for which they never paid Canada a price in the form of concessions to Canadian exporters, an advantage which those countries never expected. In brief, it was simply a windfall to them.
We cannot afford to give windfalls for nothing to other countries in terms of advantages in Canadian markets in this way. The erosion which has continued has cost and is costing jobs to many Canadians. This legislation aims at restoring those jobs to Canadians.
The issue presented by this measure is whether we wish to see unemployment in Canadian industries which, as a result of the erosion of the past decade, have lost the advantages they previously enjoyed. I say that the principle of this bill then relates to the clarification of a definition with a view to restoring the value of those provisions in the Customs Tariff to the position that they were recognized to have prior to the decade of erosion.
What, then, is the effect of the bill, Mr. Speaker? The bill-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I shall be coming back to that later, and I think I can satisfy the inquiry of the hon. member at that time.
The effect of the bill is to divide certain imported goods into two classes. First there are shelf goods and, second, there are custom made goods according to specifications. As to the shelf goods which, of course, will be in the majority, the measure will provide that goods will be deemed to be of a class or kind made in Canada if goods of approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada. There is a condition that they shall not be so deemed to be of a class or kind made in Canada unless at least 10 per cent of the normal Canadian consumption thereof is made or produced in Canada. In this respect the condition which now is to be found in order in council No. 1618 of July 2, 1936, will be made in effect a matter of statutory enactment instead of executive decree, which it has been ever since 1936.
As to the second class of goods, namely those custom made according to specifications, goods of this nature will be deemed of a class or kind made in Canada if adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.
There is a condition applicable to both the shelf goods and those custom made according to specifications. The goods may be deemed to be of a class or kind not made or produced in Canada where similar goods made or produced in Canada are not offered for sale to the ordinary agencies for wholesale or retail distribution, or are not offered to all purchasers on equal terms under like conditions having regard to the custom and usage of trade.
Sir, the reasons for separating goods into two classes are obvious. The provisions for determining whether goods are to be deemed to be of a class or kind made in Canada are sound and reasonable. They will provide what, in the light of the erosion of the past decade, as a result of decisions, has been badly needed; namely, first a clear definition and, second, a restoration of the law as it was previously construed and applied before this decade of erosion. With the enactment of this measure, Mr. Speaker, we shall have for the first time a positive definition where previously there has been merely a negative limitation.
My next observation concerns the method of determination. Under the present law the decisions of the deputy minister of national

revenue are subject to an appeal which lies to the tariff board; that is to say, appeals from his decision with respect to whether goods are or are not of a class or kind made in Canada. The tariff board conducts hearings of such cases, in the legal expression, de novo. The appeals are not argued from the record in the previous stage of proceedings. A further appeal lies from the decision of the tariff board to the Exchequer Court of Canada on a question of law; similarly, an appeal lies from the decision of the Exchequer Court of Canada to the Supreme Court of Canada on a question of law. Both in the Exchequer Court and in the Supreme Court of Canada, of course, the appeal is argued from the record; there is no hearing de novo.
This bill makes no reference whatever to the subject of appeal. It does not abolish the right of appeal on findings on the question whether goods are of a class or kind made in Canada, but it does provide quite simply that as to three elements in such cases the decision of the Minister of National Revenue shall be final.
These three elements are, first, whether the goods in question are shelf goods or are custom made according to specifications; second, if they are shelf goods, what is the normal consumption thereof in Canada; third, as to the other class of goods, namely those goods made according to specifications, whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production thereof within a reasonable period of time. A full right of appeal continues with respect to leading elements such as the following: first, whether or not the imported shelf goods are of approximately the same class or kind as goods made in Canada; second, the determination of the amount of Canadian production; third whether or not the number of articles manufactured in Canada does in fact constitute a minimum of 10 per cent of normal Canadian consumption.
Under the provisions of the bill in the matters I have just now mentioned the house will recognize the advantage that the bill offers in that it will simplify procedure and expedite decision, and this will react to the advantage of business, including Canadian importers. Under the present law, with its uncertainties, there have been some very long delays, drawn out procedures, and great uncertainties which have been harmful to business operations.
Sir, as to some of the criticisms that have been heard in this regard, I should like to say at once that in my respectful submission there has been a great deal of exaggeration and misunderstanding. We are not taking

away the right of appeal. The bill will provide that with respect to three matters the decision of the minister in such appeal shall be taken to be final. In these three elements the minister is in the best position to make these determinations. They are largely on statistical questions, and moreover depend very largely on confidential information obtained from those engaged in business and trade, information that they are often quite loath to put forward in a public hearing before the tariff board because that information is frequently of advantage to their competitors.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have to say that there has been a great deal of exaggeration in the views that have been expressed on this subject. Perhaps what has been said today will help to clarify the terms of the bill in this regard.
It has been suggested, Mr. Speaker, that there is something arbitrary about the kind of provisions that are contained in this measure. Well, one does not hear ringing cries that there has been arbitrary legislation enacted in similar respects by the mother of parliaments at Westminster. Let me draw attention to the kind of legislation that the mother of parliaments has passed in regard to this subject, and the method of determination that is provided under the United Kingdom legislation. I shall be reading certain extracts from a document issued by the board of trade and the commissioners of customs and excise of the United Kingdom. It is notice No. 339 for the year 1960. This is the way in which the law is described in this official publication of the government of the United Kingdom. The first extract relates to the provisions of the law itself, and reads as follows:
1. Law. (a) Liability to duty.-Under the import duties act, 1958, protective duties are normally chargeable on imported machinery in order to protect United Kingdom machinery manufacturers.
(b) Duty free admission.-Section 6 of the 1958 act and paragraph 1(b) of the fourth schedule thereto . . . provide that the treasury may, on the recommendation of the board of trade, direct that payment shall not be required of any duty chargeable under section 1 of the 1958 act on particular importations of machinery, (other than aircraft and parts or equipment for incorporation in or use on aircraft) if similar articles are not for the time being procurable in the United Kingdom. If duty has been paid on importation, the duty may be repaid under a treasury direction.
So you see, Mr. Speaker, that the law is quite comparable with ours and the provision that is made for customs duty on importation, whether it is at the low rate or at the higher rate, is a matter for decision by the treasury on the recommendation of the board of trade. I have not heard anybody complaining about there not being an effective right of appeal there when both the treasury 90205-6-235J
Customs Tariff
and the board of trade are represented by their ministers in the House of Commons and can be called to account at any time.
I turn to page 4 of this interesting publication under the heading "The 'Similarity' Condition".
(a) General.-The similarity of machines for the purposes of compliance with the statutory condition referred to in paragraph 1(b) is judged primarily in relation to the product or effect and the efficiency with which it is produced. The appearance, size, shape, method of producing the given product or effect and the cost of machines are not regarded as relevant. To justify a recommendation for remission of the protective duty, it must be shown that the foreign machine has a definite and marked superiority in performance over any comparable machine procurable in the United Kingdom. Where such superiority cannot be shown to exist in general performance, application for remission of duty may be made on the ground that the machine has a definite and marked superiority in performance for the particular use for which the user requires it, provided that it is to be employed to a very substantial extent on the work for which it has such superiority.
On the same page paragraph 7 deals with application on the grounds of long United Kingdom delivery, and reads as follows:
Applications for remission of duty on grounds of long United Kingdom delivery will be entertained only if the user of the machine submits evidence to show that when he placed the order for the foreign machine:
(a)	no manufacturer in the United Kingdom could deliver a similar machine within two years; and
(b)	where delivery by United Kingdom manufacturers was
(i)	between 24 and 30 months, the foreign delivery was within 15 months; or
(ii)	more than 30 months, the foreign delivery was within one half of the United Kingdom delivery period.
It will be observed that the conditions for qualifying for the application of the lower rate of duty are much more rigid and difficult of compliance under the United Kingdom legislation than they are under the Canadian legislation, and the decisions in these matters rest with the treasury on the recommendation of the board of trade. So much for the allegations that this legislation is of an arbitrary nature.
I was asked at an earlier stage of the session to give some information concerning appeals pending before the tariff board. The total number of appeal cases registered but not heard before the tariff board on the date on which this information was obtained and given to the house, March 8, 1961, was 69, and of these 69 cases I was informed that 20 might have some relationship to the question of class or kind. There were 17 of these 20 cases that were, I am informed, considered as straight class or kind cases, and there were three others in which the tariff classification,

Customs Tariff
directly or indirectly, possibly might involve the question of whether the goods were of a class or kind made in Canada.
As to those 20 cases, 17 plus 3, I have this further breakdown. In 18 cases the goods were clearly shelf goods within the definition in the bill now before us. One involved goods that under the bill would clearly be custom made according to specifications, and the other case was one in which, I am told, the goods were probably of a kind that would be ruled to be custom made according to specifications under the present bill.
Then there is a further breakdown with respect to those 20 cases pending at March 8. It is a breakdown on the basis of whether or not they would be affected by the proposed amendments to the Customs Tariff in the present bill. I am advised that of the 20 it is quite clear that 18 would not be affected by the bill. One is clearly a case where the decision of the minister, if made under the bill, would be final with respect to the point under appeal, and with respect to the other one of the 20 cases the status was doubtful.
Let me offer a further observation concerning the volume of these appeals. In the calendar year 1960 there were 39 decisions by the tariff board on appeals. Of those 39, 28 related to decisions with respect to class or kind. Of these, only two involved goods that would be interpreted under the present bill as custom made according to specifications. The explanation for the unusually large number of class or kind decisions in 1960 is that from May, 1954 until the Supreme Court of Canada gave its decision in the power shovels case on October 7, 1958 the board virtually ceased hearing appeals involving class or kind questions pending the judgment of the higher courts. It was hoped that the courts or parliament would provide proper criteria, a proper interpretation that would assist the tariff board in future cases of the same kind. But, Mr. Speaker, no assistance was received in this regard from the decisions of the courts and it is needful, therefore, that parliament now supply what is lacking, and what is so obviously lacking, in the way of definition and restoration.
In almost all "class or kind" appeals the issue for decision has involved the question of whether the imported goods were or were not of the same class or kind as the Canadian goods; that is to say, the issue of what were the appropriate limits of the expression "class or kind". There have been very few cases where, having determined the appropriate limit of the term "class or kind", the issue turned on whether the Canadian production constituted more or less than 10 per cent of consumption. One such case, and the only one I have been able to discover in which
the issue comes out clearly in the published decision, relates to certain truck cranes, decision No. A-471, dated June 22, 1960.
In this particular case the board accepted, with some publicly expressed misgivings, and used confidential information submitted to it by the department. The board also obtained certain confidential information itself. The board found its own efforts to compile data on consumption difficult, time consuming and not satisfactory. I have the following quotation, Mr. Speaker, from the board's report in this case, and it is informative. I quote:
At the hearing, counsel for the department requested the board to receive certain evidence in confidence under the terms of subsection 10 of section 5 of the Tariff Board Act. Counsel for the appellant objected to this procedure. After hearing argument from all counsel and assuring itself that the information was indeed "in its nature confidential", the board received the evidence in confidence.
While the board is empowered to receive information that is in its nature confidential it is very much aware of the dangers and difficulties that may be associated with the practice of receiving evidence in confidence.
Accordingly, it would hope that in the future counsel would reach an agreement, as they have been able to do in the past, that would enable the board to come to a decision on the basis of evidence that is not confidential.
Just for the information of hon. members, would the minister indicate either the names of the parties concerned or the nature of the product over which the dispute took place?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I indicated that the nature of the product was truck cranes.
It will be quite clearly apprehended by the house, Mr. Speaker, from that quotation that the board has itself recognized the difficulties that confronted it in making a determination based upon confidential information. This is the type of difficulty that the present bill is intended to overcome. It will obviously be of assistance to the board in that regard.
The real cause of this difficulty that is mentioned, apart from the problem of obtaining information that is available only in confidence, is the non-existence of appropriate official statistics. Reference has been made to this subject earlier, Mr. Speaker. I simply comment briefly on it now by saying that in most cases the dominion bureau of statistics returns do not give a breakdown in sufficient detail to make available the information required for the establishment of the "normal Canadian consumption". The latter figure is obtained by adding imports to the Canadian production and reducing this total by the exports.
I was asked a question concerning this matter of erosion. Here I should like to give the house the benefit of some study that has

been devoted to that question. I reaffirm that the words "class or kind", as I have said in earlier stages, were intended to be given a reasonably broad interpretation; that in fact they were consistently interpreted broadly until 1950; that during the period since 1950 former departmental interpretations have been narrowed considerably as a result of certain tariff board declarations, and that the effect has been to erode to some extent the protection afforded Canadian producers.
Reference has been made to certain tariff board cases. In his speech on February 20, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River quoted extensively from two tariff board declarations relating to power shovels. These were dated April 18, 1953 and May 20, 1954 respectively. He drew from them the comforting conclusion that there has been no erosion or narrowing of the class or kind concept.
I regret that I must profoundly disagree with the hon. member. I say instead that these two cases really demonstrate that the class or kind concept had not been narrowed to the same extent in 1953 or 1954 as it has more recently. This may be illustrated by reference to the 1960 case, appeal No. 450, to which he referred later in his speech.
In this connection it is of interest to compare the issues which were at stake in 1953 and 1954 with those which were at stake in 1960. The issue presented to the tariff board for decision in 1953 was whether all power shovels, without regard to size, should be treated as a single class or kind, or whether it was proper for the Department of National Revenue to apply the range principle and to rule separately in respect of a certain range of sizes of shovels. The effect of the 1953 declaration was to endorse the "range" principle, under which the department had ruled that a certain range of shovels, as measured by dipper capacity, were made in Canada and that sizes outside this range were "not made". This decision was without prejudice to what constituted the proper range of sizes.
The second power shovel case, that is appeal No. 306, on which the tariff board declaration is dated May 20, 1954, had the effect of confining the limits of the range of sizes deemed to be of a class or kind made in Canada. In this case the tariff board decided that it was not legitimate to include in the range of sizes deemed to be "made in Canada" any competitive products of sizes larger or smaller than the largest or smallest sizes actually made in Canada. Thus this 1954 decision maintained the range principle, but at the same time cast doubt upon a number of earlier departmental rulings declaring broad classes of goods to be made in Canada without
Customs Tariff
reference to the question of whether the particular sizes under review were or were not within the range of sizes being made in Canada.
I shall refer later to some of these rulings, and to early tariff board cases confirming them. The point which I make now is that the declaration in appeal No. 306 upheld the "range" principle, but that this same principle was undermined by some later decisions. One such case is the only recent case which was referred to by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River in his speech. It is the declaration dated September 12, 1960 on appeal No. 450. This relates to a tilting pan filter which had been imported on November 15, 1956. Here the range principle was not even mentioned in the decision, and the case turned on whether the differences which existed between the particular imported filter under consideration and competing Canadian filters were or were not sufficient to set the imported filter apart as being of a different class or kind from those made in Canada.
The board, in effect, decided that this particular filter did constitute a different class or kind. The inference is that under the existing language of the Customs Tariff imported goods must be virtually identical with the competing Canadian goods or the special rate of duty applicable to "goods of a class or kind not made in Canada" will be applied.
Opinions may differ as to whether the board was right or wrong in this 1960 decision having regard to the language of the statute under which it had to make its decision. However, I submit that this decision to which the hon. member referred, as well as a number of other decisions to which I referred on a previous occasion, represent a serious narrowing of the class or kind concept from that which was intended and which was still being applied at the time that present GATT commitments were entered into in 1947.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate at one stage remarked that he would wish to be satisfied by concrete illustrations of what the erosion actually amounted to. I do not know whether it is too much to hope for, but I shall endeavour and continue to endeavour to satisfy him. I have reviewed the tariff board declarations relating to the class or kind cases which are on file in the Department of Finance. This review has confirmed that a substantial amount of erosion has occurred to date, and that there exists a serious danger of still further erosion in the future if remedial action is not taken such as that which is proposed in the bill under debate.
Three class or kind appeals which were heard by the board in the years 1933 and

Customs Tariff
1934 illustrate the original concept. In each instance the tariff board upheld a departmental ruling applying a broad construction to the words "class or kind". I shall deal with these three cases in turn.
The first is appeal No. 4, concerning dolls, the declaration being dated August 18, 1933. This was the first appeal case on which the tariff board made a declaration, the first three appeals having been withdrawn. The question before the board was whether celluloid dolls which admittedly were not made in Canada were of the same "class or kind" as composition dolls, which latter were made in Canada. The tariff board sustained the department's ruling that the two kinds of dolls should be considered together and that accordingly both celluloid and composition dolls were of a class or kind made in Canada.
The second of these appeals is No. 7 concerning pocket lighters, the declaration being dated July 13, 1933. The question in this case was whether an imported pocket lighter of cheap construction was of a class or kind made in Canada. The circumstances were that no cheap lighters were made in Canada, but that more expensive and better fabricated Ronson lighters were made in Canada. The board upheld the department's ruling that both lighters were of the same class or kind.
The third of these appeals is No. 34 concerning rubber combs, and the declaration is dated March 1, 1934. The tariff board in this case dismissed an appeal from a ruling of the Department of National Revenue that hard rubber combs were of a class or kind made in Canada. The circumstances were that celluloid combs were made in Canada; hard rubber combs were not. The department ruled that both types were of the same class or kind, and the tariff board upheld that decision.
That is what the election of 1935 was about.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
During the war years and the first five years following the war the tariff board was largely inactive and very few appeals were taken to it on any subject. From 1939 to 1949 inclusive there does not appear to have been a case which is significant for our present purpose. However, for the sake of completeness I should mention that in a declaration dated December 30, 1941, in appeal No. 131, the board upheld a departmental ruling that red kidney beans were of a class or kind produced in Canada.
The next case which is relevant and the case which to my mind represents the real beginning of the process of erosion to which I have referred, is appeal No. 206, on which

the tariff board declaration is dated March 16, 1950. This was an appeal from a departmental ruling that Mossberg .22 calibre rifles, models 151M and 152 were of a class or kind made in Canada, and hence not eligible for admission under tariff item 441e. The rifles in question were of the auto-loading type. Another type of .22 repeating rifle was being made in Canada by the H. W. Cooey Machine and Arms Company Ltd. of Cobourg. The question at issue was whether or not the imported auto-loading rifles in question should be considered as of the same class or kind as the Canadian made repeating rifles of the same calibre. The board allowed the appeal from the decision of the department, thus narrowing the broad construction which the department had previously given to the phrase "class or kind". The relevant portion of the board's decision reads as follows:
Dictionary definitions of the word class indicate that it is used both in very broad and for very narrow designations, but in the context in which it is used in tariff item 441e it appears to be more or less synonymous with "kind". Consequently, in interpreting this item the board has taken cognizance of the more precise designation "kind". Autoloading rifles are of a kind not made in Canada. Accordingly the appeal is allowed.
The success of the appellants in this appeal No. 206 was, as might have been expected, followed by a good many other appeals by importers or their foreign suppliers seeking to narrow the interpretation of the expression "class or kind". As I have already said, they have met with a considerable degree of success during the years from 1950 to 1960 inclusive. I shall not attempt to review all these cases in detail, and I do not wish to suggest that all of them involved uninterrupted progress in the process of erosion. As one might expect, the process was not uniform and continuous. The trend, however, is unmistakable. I suggest that any hon. members who wish to pursue the matter further and to evaluate for themselves both the general trend and the cross currents might consult the declarations of the tariff board in the following cases:

I have already given the committee details regarding a number of these cases and I shall not repeat what I said earlier. However, in closing I should like to add a word about the most recent declaration in the list, which is dated November 25, 1960. This case will, I think, illustrate as well as any the trend to which I have referred.
This was not an appeal by an importer from a decision of the Department of National Revenue. Rather it was a request by the deputy minister of national revenue for the board's opinion regarding the "class or kind" status of two pieces of rolling mill machinery. One of these was a combination bloom and plate mill and the other was a vertical edger. Traditionally the department had ruled all such rolling mill machinery to be "made in Canada". However, it was recognized that this traditional practice was open to challenge in the light of a number of recent tariff board decisions which had tended to narrow the interpretation of "class or kind". Accordingly, the deputy minister of national revenue referred the case to the tariff board with the following comment:
"Machinery for rolling iron or steel has consistently been ruled to be dutiable under tariff item 427, as of a class or kind made in Canada. The importer claims entry of the above equipment under tariff item 427a, as machinery of a class or kind not made in Canada."
In its declaration which, as I have said, is dated November 25, 1960, the tariff board noted that both bloom mills and plate mills
Customs Tariff
are made in Canada, and that at least one combination mill, although of smaller size, had been made in Canada. However, it found that the particular Blaw-Knox combination mill in question differed in a number of respects from any rolling mill which had been made in Canada as of that date. While there was no suggestion that the mill in question could not be built in Canada, the fact was that no identical or virtually identical mill had been made here. Accordingly, the imported mill in question was declared to be of a class or kind not made in Canada. This declaration, which, as I have said, is the most recent declaration available on a "class or kind" case, provides a further example of the erosion to which I have referred. Its effect was to admit under tariff item 427a at a reduced rate of duty a rolling mill which under the traditional departmental practice followed prior to the decade of erosion would have been classified under tariff item 427 as part of the broad category "machinery for rolling iron or steel" and probably would have been so considered even far into the period of that decade before the process of erosion had run the full course it has now done.
I shall not detain the house further in moving the second reading of this bill. This is a bill which in my respectful submission is urgently needed to bring some assistance to the tariff board in the nightmare in which it has found itself as a result of the course of decisions, and to supply what parliament ought in any circumstances to supply in connection with legislation of this kind, namely a clear definition.
In addition to supplying that clear definition-a positive definition for the first time- this bill will also bring about one other necessary result, and that is the restoration of the legislation to the effect that it was always understood to have prior to what I have called the decade of erosion. Here is a situation in which Canadian workmen have been deprived over the years, and particularly in these latter years, of the benefit of legislation which parliament certainly intended for them and which they enjoyed from the time that this legislation first became effective in 1907 in Mr. Fielding's tariff of that year right down to these recent years. Surely it is their right to have the benefit of that legislation restored to them, particularly when the jobs of Canadians are at stake in the issue.

I think it was the Dominion Engineering Company. Anyway, I did give the details at that time. The premier of Quebec was present. That was five years after the appeal and it was stated that it had taken that length of time before such a shovel could be produced in Canada.

The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton suggests he has a little machine shop capable of doing the work. I do, however, have some information at hand with respect to the case which, I think in the words of the minister, was the classic or basic case which in his view started the erosion over the past decade. He referred to the automatic .22 rifle case of 1950. Here again we are being invited to repeat ourselves because the minister made no reference whatsoever in his presentation to the house this afternoon to the practice which I outlined during the previous stage of the debate, namely the opportunity that goes to the department itself to make what are called "made in Canada" rulings.
In connection with the .22 rifles' case, the Department of National Revenue had on its books what I think at that time was the last ruling with respect to .22 rifles, a ruling dated 1939. That makes clear a policy of that department which did not accept a range of interpretation because the department was bound by the law of parliament. The law of parliament said that there must be actual production in Canada equal to 10 per cent of Canadian consumption of the particular kind of article that was being imported and being assessed for duty. According to my information it was not until the very day that the appeal was launched in connection with the .22 rifles' case that the Department of National Revenue decided to change its 1939 rulings. I think that new ruling is dated March 16, 1950. This subject could, however, be dealt with in some detail at a subsequent stage of the debate.
The minister again today advances his adherence to GATT. I propose to have something further to say about that this afternoon.
The minister also again refers to appeals, and I propose to have something to say about that in proper sequence later this afternoon, because I think perhaps the public of Canada is more aroused about the taking of this arbitrary power

instead of it being subject to the law of the land and the course of that law-and placing it in the hands of one single minister.
It is sometimes suggested, Mr. Speaker, that there is no consequential difference any more between the party that sits to your right and the party which sits to your left with respect to the administration of tariffs. I think this particular legislation and the legislation that was introduced in 1958, which

again gave very fantastic power to an individual minister, indicate very clearly the traditional difference in tariff administration between the political parties of this country. It is not just coincidence that every time a change of government has occurred during the last 40 years we have found one government reversing the policy of the other an example of which we have here, an instance involving the abolishment of appeals from ministerial decision. This happened in 1921 when we had legislation introduced by Mr. Meighen. It was repealed immediately by the Mackenzie King administration which came into office in 1921. In 1930 the King administration introduced sections 427 and 427(a), regarding the machinery items which the Minister of Finance indicates to us are the most important items which are involved in the legislation that is before us today. In the same year, when the Bennett administration came into office, it cancelled that legislation of the Mackenzie King administration, and when Mackenzie King succeeded Mr. Bennett in 1935 and initiated subsequently the Canadian-United States trade treaty, sections 427 and 427(a) relating to machinery were restored.
We have here, as a result of this proposed legislation, a new Conservative government attempting to erode the meaning, habit and practice with respect to the administration of these items. Notwithstanding what I have said, the minister has said that he is doing no more in this legislation than returning to an historical interpretation and concept. The minister made this assertion in substance today and certainly specifically with the introduction of the supplementary budget on December 20, as reported at page 1013 of Hansard.
I have indicated that this machinery legislation was introduced by Mr. Dunning, who was the minister of finance in the Mackenzie King administration of 1930. The present Minister of Finance, on December 20 in his speech as reported in Hansard at page 1013, had this to say:
The purpose of these items, as stated at the time the most important of them were originally established, was to provide for reduced rates of duty on "machinery or production, not procurable in Canada".
According to my research, it was in 1930 in Mr. Dunning's speech that this phrase "not procurable in Canada" was first used. I want to suggest that is perhaps the origin of this phrase in parliamentary debate.
When Mr. Dunning introduced the items 427 with respect to machinery, he had this to say, as reported in Hansard of May 1, 1930 at

All other machinery-including engines and boilers and electrical apparatus-imports of which amount to scores of millions of dollars, and a great part of which is machinery or production, not procurable in Canada, is divided into two classes-* made in Canada and not made in Canada; the former group is slightly increased under the general tariff; the latter is reduced under all tariffs and made free under the British preference. Among the machinery and equipment in this latter class which formerly was dutiable and is now made free under the British preferential tariff, are included:

The Minister of Finance has been making some very positive statements across the country, since the budget was introduced, as to the innocence of this legislation, and I think he must have given this indication to his followers in some private conversations in caucus because very few of them have offered protests, as I would have expected. The minister in a speech to the Empire Club of Winnipeg on February 10, 1961 had the following to say:
Let me speak now of the measures proposed in the supplementary budget regarding the provisions in the Customs Tariff relating to goods of a "class or kind" made in Canada. I do so because these proposals have been subjected to erroneous interpretation and baseless charges of protectionism.
Well, let us have a look at this matter of "baseless charges of protectionism."

I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that, having read these positive assertions by the Minister of Finance, there is indeed a big gap between rhetoric and reality.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And the hon. gentleman is proving it.

What we are finding here, as I have indicated in reviewing the history of the past 40 years, is this government again nailing its colours to the old Tory mast of Mr. Meighen and Mr. Bennett, and I am going to have something to say about its adherence to the spirit of GATT.
The minister says there is no increase in protection. He has also gone on to say that there is only one organ in the country that is responsible for some flurry in this connection. In Winnipeg in February he blamed this so-called bogey on the Winnipeg Free Press. Let us have a look at some recent thoughts of the minister himself with respect to these tariff changes. In 1959, when he introduced his budget, he said, as reported at page 2423 of Hansard:
I have been giving thought to various representations that have been made to the government regarding a very important concept which runs through our Customs Tariff: the concept that the protection afforded to goods which are ruled by the Department of National Revenue or the courts to be of a "class or kind" made in Canada should receive greater protection than similar goods of a "class or kind" not made in Canada. This differentiation, based on "class or kind", is to be found in many individual tariff items and also in our antidumping and countervailing duties.
Some of the representations have suggested legislation which would define or re-deflne the words "class or kind" in such a way as to enlarge the range of goods that are now deemed to be made in this country and thus given the greater protection. It is questionable, however, whether an overriding measure, involving a departure from present practices and present interpretations, is in the national interest.
Two years later however he is doing exactly that, and in 1959 he gave no hint that he had any conception that the "practices and interpretations" were in any way eroding the intent of parliament.
I noted this afternoon when the minister spoke that two out of three of the important cases he cited as indicative of the law prior to this erosion were decisions from the tariff board during the regime of the former Conservative government under R. B. Bennett. Perhaps there might later be some erosion with respect to the practices of the tariff board during the Bennett regime to which two out of three of these cases he cited relate, and I propose to deal with the third one on another occasion. This seems to differ very radically from the stand taken by the Minister of National Revenue in the debate on a previous stage of this debate. At that time the Minister of National Revenue did

not suggest that we must find a remedy for erosion relating to the tariff board practices under Mr. R. B. Bennett. What the Minister of National Revenue had to say to us and presumably particularly to the members of the Conservative party who represent ridings that know it is not in their interests to fight tariffs, was: "Don't be alarmed; we are simply making sure that the type of tariff administration as practised under Mackenzie King is not going to remain eroded." I found this afternoon that two of the three cases were heard in the 1930's when the Bennett administration was in power.
The minister says no tariff increase is involved. I think it would be appropriate to show what some independent thinkers have to say. The minister and I had some discussion at the previous stage when he said, "Oh, you are just carrying on the harangue of the Winnipeg Free Press". I indicated at that time that I would be very pleased to quote at the appropriate time not the Winnipeg Free Press but its opposition in the city of Winnipeg, the Winnipeg Tribune, and I do so now. The exchange between the minister and myself took place on February 15, as reported at page 2086 of Hansard. The extract from the Tribune reads in part as follows:
Class or kind-
The proposed "class or kind" changes In the tariff are running into stiff opposition in the House of Commons-and so they should. The changes are objectionable on two main scores: first, they are clearly protectionist and designed to restrict trade; second, the amendments, if approved in their present form, would give the minister authority to make arbitrary decisions against which there could be no appeal.
The proposed changes would virtually destroy the individual's right of appeal. The minister's decision on custom made goods-a term covering a large volume of imports-would be final. In practice this would mean that a customs officer would make rulings which could not be challenged in the courts or before an appeal board.
The Winnipeg Tribune went on to say that the federal government has taken some pride in the fact that in 1960 its exports have expanded. They point out that those exports expanded while the former law was prevailing, and the Tribune reminds the administration that trade is a two-way street, and it says that if Canada imposes restrictions, even hidden restrictions such as involved here, other countries will reply in kind and Canada will be the loser.
There are people other than the Free Press and hon. members of the opposition who sense in this legislation a very important hike in protectionism, and an unknown hike because it is to be operated in the office of the minister and in large part without appeal. The Globe and Mail of March 13, 1961 -and this newspaper is published in the

midst of the Ontario manufacturing industry -had this to say respecting this Customs Tariff amendment:
This amendment would deprive importers of their right of appeal, in these cases, to either the courts or the tariff board. It is impossible to see any justification for this. The questions to be decided are matters of fact, whether, for example, Canadian industry can really produce a particular article in a reasonable period of time. Issues of this kind are properly settled not by a harassed cabinet minister-[DOT]
Like the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan).

No. I continue:
-but by an impartial tribunal which has heard both sides. In the course of the debate on the amendment in the House of Commons earlier this month, opposition speakers also pointed out that it infringed parliament's control over taxation and trade. In effect it gives the Minister of National Revenue power to increase tariffs without the consent of parliament.
Other important journals have expressed a similar view, one of which is the Financial Post, and I may say that I am not speaking today from the point of view of my western background.
Western? How far west?

My present residence is reasonably west, being west of the lakehead, but I was born and raised on the prairies and I have a great affection for that part of Canada. The Financial Post had this to say in an editorial:
The switch from administrative or departmental decisions, which can be appealed, to ministerial decisions, which cannot, opens the way to all sorts of undesirable developments. If, when ruling on such a customs case, the revenue minister accepted regularly, without question, the advice and decisions of his civil servants, we would get government by bureaucracy.
That is the kind of thing about which we used to hear when my hon. friends opposite were sitting on this side of the house. The editorial goes on to say:
If one minister after another did throw in his two cents worth, we would very likely get inconsistencies and capriciousness in a very complicated, very sensitive area. Finally, ministerial decision which cannot be appealed makes possible government behind the public's back, changes in tariffs without changes in tariff legislation.
Long before the legislation was introduced a good journalistic friend of the present government who represents another eastern newspaper in the press gallery, the Montreal Gazette, a newspaper generally recognized for its Conservative adherence, had something to say about this matter. I refer to Arthur Blakely who, having read the speech from the throne, had this to say:

Large sections of Canadian industry, which have been pressing the government hard this past year for additional tariff protection, are persuaded that these sentences in the throne speech were designed as an answer to their prayers.
The Montreal Star made this comment in an editorial on December 28, 1960:
Much, of course, will depend on the way in which the new powers are used, but it seems fairly definite that the government has embarked on an openly protectionist course.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that not only does this legislation involve opportunities, such as we know were taken advantage of in the thirties by the Bennett administration, for the ministerial hiking of effective tariff rates to mountainous levels but these rates can be set in a cunning, clandestine and cabalistic manner. In addition, members of this ministry in their explanation throughout the country of what is involved in this legislation have brought about as usual a great confusion and conflict. I have quoted what the Minister of Finance said in Winnipeg. I find that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) told his constituents that the activities of the government involved no increase in protection. He made the same assertion in that western area of Canada as did the Minister of Finance on February 10.

Mr. Hees said yesterday that the class or kind legislation which is now before parliament would impose or raise tariffs on foreign goods closely similar to those made in Canada, and should thus increase domestic sales of the Canadian-made product.
The Globe and Mail made this comment in its editorial:
This is simply another way of saying that foreign goods closely similar to those made in Canada are cheaper than those made in Canada.
I have been greatly disappointed at the silence of so many of my colleagues in the House of Commons who, I know, will not find that this legislation is in the interests of their constituencies. The Minister of Finance indicated that the major item here has to do with machinery. When he was asked whether it would not be wise to allow an appeal to the tariff board so that we could be sure that all the facts would be made fully known he said, "Oh, no, the administration is a relatively simple matter". He said that, after all, there were only eight or ten plants involved and that they could check on them through the Department of National

-which, if won by those promoting increases, may well put many western grain farmers out of business, cause more suffering in the already ailing Alberta coal industry and, above all, create even higher unemployment at a time when more Canadians are out of jobs than at any time since the second world war at this time of year.
I indicated I was disappointed that this silent and slavish group of back bench members should support this legislation which I submit will not be of any benefit to the vast number of constituencies which they represent and will in fact be harmful. I notice the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) smiling as I proceed with my remarks.

I say to them that it has been quite a spectacle to find that the Vancouver board of trade, the British Columbia Electric Company, the B.C. loggers' association, the truck loggers' association and a number of other producers' organizations of this kind have had to depend for advocacy so far as this matter is concerned on the C.C.F. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and the C.C.F. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. 
Regier) who are the only ones from British Columbia who have spoken for them on this matter.
Perhaps the people who spoke like that western member have changed their views because they did not know what was likely to happen this session. Apparently the high protectionists, to whom that member referred, have won out and they decided to jettison the policy they had in mind and just continue to follow John. Even some hon. members who think this legislation might be of some benefit to their ridings are in for some striking disappointments. I do not know whether or not their own research is responsible for some of the misconceptions they have or whether these misconceptions result from the blandishments they have received from members of the ministry who say, "This is fine for you; this is going to do a job for your friends".
The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Smith) was one of the few who had anything to say in this debate, other than those who have official responsibility for the measure. You will recall that on February 27 he was filled with joy. The thought that the manufacturers of heavy chains, made in his riding, would receive some benefit from the measure. He referred to tire chains for tractors and to another manufacturing plant that is manufacturing automatic transmissions. This bill gave him some heart and some courage. I suppose his feelings have been echoed in the Conservative caucus, and those backbenchers with these hopes evidently outnumbered those who could see danger in this legislation.
Let us look at the situation in so far as heavy chains are concerned. I am informed that heavy chains would be interpreted as shelf goods in accordance with section 2 (a) (2) of the new legislation and therefore would have to be produced to the extent of 10 per cent of the normal Canadian consumption. I am informed that the bill we have before us will not help the manufacturers of tire chains for tractors because these chains enter duty free under item 409n as accessories for tractors. In so far as automatic transmissions are concerned, I am informed that under this legislation there is no help for industrial ridings such as Lincoln because the drawback duty is not payable on automatic transmissions. If the hon. member really wants some help in respect of the manufacturing of automatic transmissions, I am afraid he has to go to tne government he supports and ask that government to cancel the legislation that it brought in by order in council on November 1, 1959. This legislation allows transmissions to enter Canada free. I think disillusionment

will be found in the Tory caucus if hon. members who have presented both points of view there will give this bill further study.
I said it was my intention to say something about the minister's continuous, loud declarations of his adherence to GATT, both in a technical sense and in spirit. We are all very familiar with these resounding declarations of rectitude that constantly flow from the Minister of Finance. Perhaps we should further examine this declaration. On December 20, as reported on page 1014 of Hansard, the minister did actually admit, in mild language, that retaliation against our exports was possible. He tried to persuade us that it was not probable. The minister is not one, in my opinion, who is given to understatement. He is generally prepared to attack a tack with a sledge-hammer. In his speech to the Canadian club at Toronto on January 9, 1961, I think perhaps the minister made, for him, the understatement of 1961. He said:
While this action has aroused the interest of our associates in the GATT, we are confident that it is within its framework.
I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to other members of this house that a great deal more than interest has been aroused by this legislation, especially in so far as our best customers, the United States and the United Kingdom, are concerned. I raised this subject by way of a formal question on the order paper on March 8, and again received a rather bland, evasive, innocent sounding statement from the minister, as reported on page 2774 of Hansard for that date. He said:
-no contracting parties signatory to the general agreement on tariffs and trade. .. have intimated to Canadian government representatives in Canada or abroad that they will expect Canada to negotiate compensatory tariff adjustments or give trade concessions in the event that the Customs Tariff is amended in accordance with the terms outlined in a resolution therefor introduced by the Minister of Finance on December 20, 1960.
This is the brush-off. This is the indication not to look under the rug. The minister went on to say:
There have been discussions, as I think I intimated on an earlier occasion, with both the United Kingdom and the United States governments concerning the significance of the proposed amendment. Some of these discussions actually date back to the time before the terms of the proposed amendment were made known.
The United Kingdom government has intimated that it will be interested in the administration of the proposed amendment, and reserves whatever rights it may possess.
No indication is given in that statement as to the action the United States may take. As I pointed out at a previous stage of the debate, this legislation removes the right of appeal from the board to our courts which, as I read the GATT agreement, is mandatory. In fact, this measure removes in large part

the type of appeal that had been operative for almost 15 years before GATT and about 13 years after GATT.
The Minister of Finance may think that these people are paying no attention to these administrative alterations in our Customs Tariff which relate to entries involving hundreds of millions of dollars. I am not so sure. I believe this government will get plucked to its pinfeathers as it proceeds with this matter in an age when more liberal trading seems to be the operation of the day for practically every other country with whom we do big business. During the debate in replying to the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Pitman) the minister suggested that activities such as are proposed here probably had a great appeal and a great advantage to labour.

They said that if we advance too aggressively in matters such as these our friends, the United States, would retaliate in their trading relations and would knock the stuffing out of us.
