It is raising it from 7i per cent to 22| per cent.

There is a 15 per cent hike on a substantial portion, as I say, of hundreds of millions of dollars of potential trade particularly between our two big customers, namely the United States and the United Kingdom. As we found previously, it is rather an invidious position to be in in the opposition to find out whose ox is going to be gored in these tariff negotiations. We are obliged to enquire respecting public hearings down in Washington to find out there what GATT proposals Canada has made, and who Canada is selling out for the purpose of giving some benefit to the eight or ten particular industries which I have indicated seem to be at the very core of the advantages involved here.
This happened in 1958. Then the Minister of Finance would not make available to us any information as to what quid pro quo was likely to follow with respect to these partners of ours in GATT that would require compensation. I suggest that we are going to find retaliation here. If we do not find it directly, we are going to find that it is less easy for us in the immediate future to negotiate with these countries on further proposals that might be to our advantage in the matter of the liberalization of trade. The Minister of Finance seems to want to keep this retaliation skeleton in his closet, but it will come out. Unfortunately we will find who has paid for these concessions. We will find that only by going over to Washington where these things are discussed publicly or we shall have to have somebody who visits Geneva tell us, from the negotiations that are still carrying on there under GATT, what the sacrifices in Canada by exporters are likely to be.
Since we discussed some of these matters in the committee of ways and means, a delegation of the ministers of this government went down to Washington. I think my point is fairly conclusively established in this understanding assembly when I quote what the usual vigorously speaking Minister of Finance had to say as to the attitude of the United States while there. If he had completely sold the United States on the idea that this proposal was innocent in so far as our intercountry trade was concerned and in so far as it affected them, we know that he would be the first to make quite a noise about it. But instead of that-and as I say, contrary to his usual style-we find this, and again I quote from a reporter friendly to the minister namely a reporter of the Toronto 
Globe and Mail in Washington. He quotes the Minister of Finance as summing up after the conference as follows:
The Canadian delegation has done all anybody could do to make It clear that redefining of "a class or kind made in Canada" was entirely a proper action for the Canadian government to take.
I think we can all judge what that really meant from the point of view of convincing that conference. I suggest that the real operation resulting from this legislation will be something that the ministry traditionally- or at least it is traditional with them-will tell us nothing about while this debate is on, but that the real battle will take place abroad in Geneva in ensuing days and weeks. There is not any wonder why this would not now take place there. We know that there were protests-and formal protests that time-in 1958 when the Customs Act was amended. Before any legislation was presented and simply on the knowledge that it was likely to be presented, the United States formally wrote our government and indicated their interest. There was no reply. After the legislation of 1958 was introduced they received no reply to a protest. Of course, the government's explanation was that this was correspondence between a junior in the United States embassy and a junior in the Department of External Affairs and that it got overlooked.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Like Eldorado.

Yes, like Eldorado. It turns out that the Canadian junior happens to be of the status of one of our foreign ambassadors; and it happens that the United States junior who wrote the letter is still the senior man representing the United States in this country in commercial matters.
The Minister of National Revenue is one of those who went down to Washington at this time. I can understand why now there was no need for the United States government to write letters to the Canadian government that are likely to be pigeonholed. As the minister has said the United States people have been in contact with the government and its officials informally. They are simply putting in a caveat, as one might say. They know that the real negotiations in so far as any effect on them is concerned will, as I say, take place on foreign soil and until all is a fait accompli the members of this house will know very little about it. But the Minister of National Revenue was also down in Washington on this visit and I find him quoted as saying, "Oh, there is no discrimination here; this is not aimed at the United States". Of course, there is no discrimination here. It is not aimed at the United States; it is aimed at everybody. The idea is to shut out all trade

partners. But the people affected of course are our two major customers, namely the United Kingdom and the United States.
In addition to that, if he is quoted correctly in Washington on March 13, several weeks and months after the legislation was introduced, the Minister of National Revenue passed the buck to the opposition, as the government has often done. They say that this legislation does not amount to anything, that it is mainly a political football created by the opposition. At a previous stage of this debate I quoted from one if not two of the Canadian journalists stationed in Washington and I quoted from them at a time before the budget was introduced. I quoted from them with respect to the reaction that took place in Washington simply after reading the speech from the throne. The opposition had nothing whatever to do with that. But the headline that was provided in a Washington paper which I quoted previously under the byline of Mr. Tim Creary of the Southam newspapers was a Washington newspaper headline saying Washington was "terribly" upset by what was announced in the speech from the throne.
What the Minister of Finance is simply going to tell us here is that this is just a little matter; that this is not going to affect our trade relations very much; I want to say that this means a great deal more than what many people in the country and perhaps even in the House of Commons appreciate. It is not only the consumer interest that is affected. The interesting thing is that it perhaps affects most keenly the large and small manufacturers or at least it will harm and affect large and small manufacturers in Canada other than those eight or ten who actually make machinery in Canada, to whom I have made reference. Many of these manufacturers all struggling to export in world markets at competitive prices.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce goes out in the country and his standard speech to chambers of commerce is this. He wants to know why industry cannot compete in foreign markets as well as in our own. If these manufacturers are obliged to buy something in Canada that is of lower capacity, of inferior quality, and at a higher price than that at which their competitors in other parts of the world can buy, how do you expect them long to be able to compete with other producers in other parts of the world? What happens here as we all know, is this. Instead of being able to import from the United Kingdom or the United States the most up-to-date efficient machine that up to now has not been made in Canada but which the Minister of National Revenue in a back room is going to say henceforth could be made in
Customs Tariff
Canada, what will happen is that the cost of that tariff capital levy for machinery will go up in the case of a British machine from free to 10 per cent and 22J per cent in the case of a machine from the United States.
Many businessmen will come to the conclusion that it would be business suicide to add this tariff differential to their capital costs particularly if they must wait for lengthy periods before finding out what the tariff rate is going to be; when they have to wait for the Department of National Revenue to make these national calculations statistically. I suggest this is very undesirable legislation. Everybody who knows how the administrative machinery operates knows that this does not really mean what it says; it will not be the minister who deals with these matters. The minister is not going to be able to deal with one hundredth of the applications involved in decisions relating to whether or not an article is made in Canada. The potential manufacturers who are concerned about what it would cost them to set up a plant will find themselves at the mercy of some junior official who may be very biased and limited in his knowledge of what is going on in Canada. I say that if we are abolishing the tariff board and giving power to one minister just because we do not agree with the board's decisions it will be just as logical to say that we should abolish law appeals and allow the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) himself to deal with these vital matters. I think that would be just as logical.
Somebody said that if the Russian ambassador were listening to this debate and reported to Khrushchev that such powers were being taken by the minister here in this democracy Khrushchev might die in a fit of laughter because we hypocritically talk about dictatorial action in some other countries.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this bill be not now read a second time because of new provisions for arbitrary decisions which transfer the tariff making authority from parliament to the Minister of National Revenue, contrary to the principles of responsible government and the essential rights of parliament to tax".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I wish to submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment is out of order. It purports to be an amendment to a motion for the second reading of a bill. As you well know, sir, the kind of amendment which is in order on a motion for second reading is very limited. According to my memory of the rule it requires an assertion of a contrary principle. In my submission this is not the kind of amendment which qualifies

Customs Tariff
within the narrow provisions laid down with regard to amendments to motions for second reading.
It is a clear principle of construction that an amendment cannot be introduced if it merely asserts a negative.
In the next place, it is an equally well established rule that it is not in order to bring forward an amendment simply in order to give a reason. It is in debate that we state the reasons why we take positions for or against certain motions. It seems to me that this amendment on the face of it purports to do nothing more than that. On that account it is clearly out of order. So I think that on three grounds this amendment does not qualify within the narrow rules which have been established governing amendments to motions for the second reading of bills.

I think I can greatly assist Your Honour by bringing to your attention an amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) on September 2, 1958 which read:
That all the words alter "that" he struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"that this bill be not now read a second time because of new provisions for arbitrary valuations which transfer the tariff making authority from parliament to the minister and the cabinet contrary to the principles of responsible government and the essential right of parliament to tax."
The only difference in wording between that amendment and the amendment just moved by my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River is that the word "decisions" has been substituted for the word "valuations" after the word "arbitrary", and "and the cabinet" has been left out and "of national revenue" substituted. Precisely the same objections were advanced to that amendment by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), though not in precisely the same language, as have been advanced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to the present proposed amendment.
Mr. Speaker made a ruling on all the points which were raised by the Minister of Finance, which ruling is to be found at page 535 of the Journals for that session. I do not suppose Your Honour would wish me to read them, though I could if desired. The Speaker did rule that the amendment was completely in order and I suggest that as the present amendment is entirely on all fours with the amendment which the Speaker ruled to be in order at that time it is, of course, similarly in order. Incidentally, that earlier amendment was based on an amendment which had been moved by a very experienced parliamentarian, Mr. Stewart, and seconded by Mr. Ian Mackenzie in 1930, and it was not even challenged by the government of that day.

Perhaps I may refer briefly to the arguments presented by the minister on the point of order. The hon. gentleman said he had put forward three reasons why the proposed amendment should be ruled out of order. I may have missed one of them, but I recognized only two. The hon. gentleman argued in the first place that the amendment should offer a contrary principle. I should like to call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that a motion has often been accepted in this house calling for a six months' hoist which, in effect, is the assertion of a contrary principle.
The minister gave as a further reason why this was not in order the fact that it contained in it a reason which, in his opinion, was subject to debate and therefore ought to be included in argumentation and ought not to be the subject of amendment.
I would like to refer Your Honour to a motion that is very fundamental, namely that a bill be now referred to a standing or special committee of this house in order that this or that particular feature of the bill might be more adequately explored before the house gives second reading. We often have motions that include the reasons for putting the motions before the house, and in the light of many similar motions on second reading, in regard to which we have all had experience in this house, I suggest that the other argument put forward by the minister is completely ridiculous. I hope that Your Honour will consider the reasoning put forward by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) and myself in this regard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This amendment
ought to be considered in the light of citation 382 of Beauchesne's fourth edition which reads as follows:
382. It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from, the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill, or expressing opinions as to any circumstances connected with its introduction, or prosecution; or otherwise opposed to its progress; or seeking further information in relation to the bill by committees, commissioners, the production of papers or other evidence or the opinion of judges.
I would suggest that the proposed amendment is within these limitations being a declaration, or an opinion contrary to some provision of the bill and, therefore, I would accept the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I just say a word or two before you close this matter?
I did not have before me when I was speaking earlier, the reference to the 1958

decision from which the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) read. May I draw your attention, however, to the fact that in that case the amendment did propose to assert a contrary principle, and there was a declaration of a contrary principle. At page 537 of the Journals of the House of Commons of Canada of September 2, 1958, we have a ruling of Mr. Speaker of that day.
It was pages 534 and 535.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Speaker was also referring to a reference at page 538, where the same rule appears.
Mr. Speaker, at page 537 will be found a very good example of the assertions of a contrary principle and declaratory statement. In that situation the amendment to Bill No. C-51, moved by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) seconded by the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Bourget) read as follows:
"this house reaffirms the adherence of Canada to the spirit and objectives of GATT, which are clearly violated in provisions of this bill."
The mover put this on record as asserting a contrary principle. In my respectful submission, this present amendment does not invite the house to assert a principle. The amendment reads in part as follows:
this bill be not now read a second time because of new provisions for arbitrary decisions-
There is not even a complete sentence here in what follows, and certainly no declaration of principle. This simply purports to state a reason why the bill should not now be read a second time because of certain provisions. With all respect, Mr. Speaker, this is not an assertion of principle and does not contain a declaration such as is found at page 537 of the Journals of the House of Commons of Canada of September 2, 1958. The house is not called upon to go on record as affirming a principle that is contrary to the principle of the bill. This amendment simply asks the house to subscribe to a reason, and the reason does not even contain a statement. The words "because of" simply refer to certain provisions. With great respect, Mr. Speaker, I urge upon you that this is not the kind of provision that is contemplated in the rule respecting the assertion of contrary principles by a declaration.
At page 538 of the same volume in relation to the rules governing amendments to motions for second reading we have this principle stated:
(1) It may be declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill.
I suggest with great respect that the amendment must be a declaration of a principle and not merely a reference to a purported reason.

Mr. Speaker, since you have permitted the minister to intervene in the course of your ruling I assume I may reply to what he has said. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It appears to me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has expressed an objection which goes rather to the form of the amendment than to the substance. If I interpret correctly citation 382 of Beauchesne it would seem to me that this amendment is an opinion expressed in opposition to the bill which has been introduced and that the question of form would not matter. The amendment reads in part as follows:
-because of new provisions for arbitrary decisions which transfer the tariff making authority from parliament to the Minister of National Revenue-
It is my opinion that these words express an opinion contrary to a part of the bill and I see, therefore, no reason to refuse the amendment. I declare it in order.

Mr. Speaker, the provisions of this bill were first announced in a statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in introducing the baby budget on December 20. Since that time this legislation, or the resolution preceding it, has been discussed on a number of occasions, particularly on March 2 when the bill was given first reading. There has been a long delay between first and second readings because the government did not bring it forward. Nevertheless, the fact that almost four months have elapsed since the minister declared to the house and the country that this legislation was to be brought before parliament, and the temper of the debate that has taken place since, indicate to me that this legislation is not only unpopular and unwarranted in the opinion of the opposition

Customs Tariff
parties, but indicate, I would suggest, that the government has been rather timid in proceeding with it, and has taken, in a consistent manner, every excuse to duck bringing it forward to have it approved or dealt with long before now.
The motion that has been presented by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) is that the bill be not now read a second time because of new provisions for arbitrary decision which transfer the tariff making authority from parliament to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) contrary to the principles of responsible government and the essential rights of parliament to tax.
We in this group agree wholeheartedly with the amendment. In years gone by the present Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have been very important champions of the rights of parliament. It is strange that, after a few short years in office, they should move in such a wholesale manner to deny the rights of parliament, to deny the jurisdiction of the courts and to place in the hands of the minister widespread, arbitrary powers of tariff making which, as the amendment points out, in fact are the right to tax. This comes from hon. gentlemen who have been so loud in proclaiming their championing of the rights of parliament.
I suggest that this legislation is bad; it is repugnant to the democratic system. It is legislation that is very much out of step with the times. I noticed that the minister took a long time this afternoon to introduce the legislation in his endeavour to defend it. On other occasions he made very short statements. He brushed off opposition criticism rather lightly. But today he took a long time in an effort to try to defend and to make a case for this legislation. In making his statement I noticed that the Minister of Finance did not follow his usual practice. This afternoon the minister seemed very unsure of himself. He was not the bombastic minister that he usually is, claiming that all right is on his side. He was rather timid, cautious and mild-mannered. I suggest this is some indication that the government itself knows that this legislation is unpopular; that it is, in fact, meeting with very widespread disapproval in the country.
This legislation provides for a change in the definition of goods of a "class or kind". It provides for a change in the definition by saying:
In the case of goods other than goods custom made to specifications, goods of approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada.
As the minister has so well pointed out, by changing this definition the government

will broaden the whole range and the whole class of goods to which the higher tariff of 22J per cent instead of 7i per cent will apply.
The minister has made his case on what he really says are misjudgments of the tariff board. He has said that for the past 10 years the tariff board has been incompetent. He has criticized it very widely. He has said that the tariff board today finds itself in a nightmare. I would suggest that the minister has heaped a great deal of criticism on the board and this is a method of rectifying the situation which he claims exists. He is transferring the jurisdiction from the tariff board to the minister. We had understood that the tariff board was to be made more efficient so that it could handle appeals; that the tariff board was to be set up under a two-panel system instead of a one-panel system. It would seem to me that the government is arguing both sides of the case. It is saying it wants to streamline the tariff board procedures, and yet it is taking much of the power and jurisdiction away from the board.
I would suggest that the legislation introduced today is wrong on other counts. It is far reaching in that it gives to the Minister of National Revenue the right to decide on statistics about normal Canadian consumption, and therefore the amount of the 10 per cent, and by this means it removes a large part of the jurisdiction that has heretofore been in the hands of the tariff board.
The minister is also given the power to decide whether goods are custom made to specifications and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada. One wonders how the minister is going to have all this information when the courts, according to the Minister of Finance, are ill equipped and unable to obtain this information. The minister is going to decide whether adequate facilities exist for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time. This is very indefinite phraseology; it is not precise. Large, sweeping, arbitrary powers are placed in the hands of the Minister of National Revenue.
We think that the House of Commons should reject this legislation. We have opposed it on every occasion, at every stage. We intend to continue that opposition. We intend to move amendments at the various stages and procedures of this bill, which will demonstrate again and again our complete opposition to what is being done by this legislation.
This legislation is wrong on every count. It is protectionist legislation; it is arbitrary legislation; it takes powers away from the tariff board; it takes appeals away from the courts. It places in the hands of a minister the right to tax, the right to decide tariffs, the right to decide the 10 per cent quantity.

It takes away from parliament jurisdiction that has been parliament's for a great many years.
In recent years we have been in some difficulty with respect to our balance of payments. Our export-import situation has been rather difficult, but there is at least some evidence that it is improving. I hold in my hand the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin which sets forth our experience in 1960 in the trading field. It has this to say:
Canada's trade with other countries reached a new peak in 1960, being valued at $10,891,100,000, according to preliminary figures released today by D.B.S. This was an increase of 2.3 per cent over the 1959 value of $10,649,200,000. Total exports in 1960 were valued at $5,395,300,000, a rise of 5 per cent over the previous record attained in the preceding year, while imports at $5,495,800,000 were fractionally less than in 1959. The import balance, estimated at $100,500,000, was reduced to slightly more than a quarter of last year's total and was the lowest since 1954.
According to these figures, our trade position is improving. According to the statistics, our exports have been going up by a substantial amount over our increase in imports. Does the government feel that this desirable trend should not be continued? This legislation is opposed to this kind of trend. It is likely to reverse or will tend to reverse this kind of improvement in Canada's trade position.
The minister talks about helping industry. I suggest that to provide a general increase in tariffs will not help Canadian industry. It will merely increase the costs of Canadian industries, make it more difficult for them to compete and result in higher and higher unemployment, a higher rate of unemployment than would exist if this legislation were not passed.
When Prime Minister Macmillan was in Canada recently the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) discussed with him the attitude of the British government toward a common market. It is clear that the United Kingdom is going into the common market. It is clear that this is a great threat to Canada's export industries. The Prime Minister said he has a clear impression that the United Kingdom will not upset the trading preferences and arrangements that Canada has enjoyed with the United Kingdom in the past. That is hardly a commitment; it is hardly a firm assurance.
I wonder what the attitude of the United Kingdom is with regard to the policy of the Canadian government which we are now considering. At a time when we need good will in the United Kingdom, when we need to protect our markets in that country, this kind of legislation is a challenge to the United Kingdom to discriminate against Canada, to retaliate by equally discriminatory
Customs Tariff
measures in view of the fact that we are undertaking this kind of ill-conceived, high tariff program.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River quoted a number of newspapers, organizations and other authorities that are opposed to higher tariffs.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I indicate to the hon. member my concern about the line of his remarks now because the question is on the amendment and the only subject of the amendment is the provision to transfer authority to the minister from the tariff board. Mr. Speaker, I do not mind advice and I appreciate the tenor of your remarks. I was not intending to speak at any great length even if you had not risen, but I do want to say that during all the time I have been a member of the house the practice has been that an amendment on second reading does not result in confining the debate following the amendment to the terms of the amendment but rather on second reading a wide, general discussion of the bill is in order whether or not there is an amendment.
I think I have been very much in order although I can appreciate the desire of Your Honour and perhaps of members of the house to confine the discussion at this stage solely to the substance of the amendment. However, I do want to state that in my judgment a wide ranging debate is very much in order on second reading even when an amendment has been moved.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I must say that my impression and recollection of the rulings made by the hon. gentlemen who have held the office of Speaker in the past are not in accordance with the theory just put forward by the hon. member for Assiniboia. If he has the right to do as he suggests, we will have two wide ranging debates on the whole subject. Having in mind the purport of the amendment as I recall it, I believe that the rule is as stated by Your Honour a few moments ago, that once an amendment is moved speakers who follow are, generally speaking, confined to the wording and context of the amendment. In the past Mr. Speaker has, of course, allowed reasonable leeway but certainly there

Customs Tariff
cannot be two wide ranging debates on two separate motions before the house.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think we will gain anything by the minister persisting with this so-called point of order because he is completely wrong. Not only can there be two wide ranging debates but there may be as many as four or five. I can remember that when a certain famous bill was before the house the official opposition of the day used the technique of moving a motion that the question be now put in order that another round of speakers might join in a general debate. Over the years there has been no inclination by Speakers of the House of Commons to try to confine debates to the precise wording and scope of an amendment before the house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I add this for the benefit of the hon. member. It may be true that sometimes a general debate takes place when an amendment is being considered but that depends on the nature of the amendment itself. Some amendments may provide for the discussion of the whole subject matter of the bill but when the amendment is on a precise point, as in the present instance, I think the discussion on the amendment should be limited to its subject matter, namely, the transfer of the making of decisions from the tariff board to the Minister of National Revenue. That is the subject matter of the amendment. The hon. member may be right as to the scope of the debate in other cases but in the present case I think the debate has to be limited if the rules are to be applied.

Mr. Speaker, I submit again that it is in order to have a wide ranging debate even on an amendment such as the one now before the house. I state again that it is not my intention to make a long speech at this time. Apart altogether from your intervention, I had almost concluded my remarks and only have one or two more thoughts to leave with the house.
I was saying that this legislation is unpopular, that it provides for the giving of arbitrary powers to the minister and that it is not in keeping with the history of the Conservative party when they were in opposition. This legislation, which provides for this arbitrary transfer of powers, demonstrates that the Prime Minister has forgotten all about his campaign to protect the rights of parliament. It demonstrates that so far as this legislation is concerned the Prime Minister has abdicated his own responsibility and has surrendered it to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance, the arch-Tory of the

Tory party, has brought forward this legislation as a pay-off to the financial interests that the minister is seeking to assist by means of this legislation.
That is nonsensical.

The Prime Minister's attitude in the past has been to protect the rights of parliament. I have never known him to advocate higher tariffs in the past but apparently he has handed over his jurisdiction in this matter to the Minister of Finance who is now proceeding by this means to bring about a general increase in tariffs without any support that I know of from any major organizations in the country. Organized labour is not supporting a high tariff policy. Organized agriculture is not supporting a high tariff policy. No party in this house with the exception of the Tory party, is in favour of this kind of repugnant high tariff legislation.
That is your word for it.
I suggest the government is out of step with the kind of trade procedures that are now being followed in the world, and out of step with public opinion in Canada.

If no one has anything to say at this time, I should like to say that it seems most extraordinary to me that, in the face of an amendment of this character when there are 200 representatives in this house who are now supporting the government and the number is dwindling all the time and is likely to continue to decline as rapidly as circumstances permit, we find this sort of Quaker meeting with no one on the government side able to make any observations about this far-reaching amendment.
Maybe the amendment is not worth it.

The hon. gentleman says the amendment is not worth it. The hon. gentleman would not have said that if he had been sitting over here supporting his leader when his leader was over here. At that time there was no more ardent verbal champion of the rights of parliament than the right hon. gentleman. There has been the most extraordinary and complete metamorphosis since the right hon. gentleman crossed to the other side of the house. Nothing could better illustrate that metamorphosis than the legislation which is now before us, and particularly that feature of the legislation about which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainly River (Mr. Benidickson) has invited us to express an opinion in this amendment that is now before the house.

The amendment indicates that this legislation is unacceptable and should not be proceeded with because it makes new provisions for arbitrary decisions which transfer the tariff making authority from parliament to the Minister of National Revenue. I underline the word "new" because three years ago, over our objections, other similar provisions were made. Then the amendment goes on to point out that this is contrary to the principles of responsible government and the essential rights of parliament to tax. These principles were always respected by Liberal governments. The very basis of our constitution is that taxes should be imposed not by one of the 265 representatives of the people but by all of them or by a majority of them after due deliberation and debate.
What this government is seeking to do by this legislation is to permit one minister, not even the governor in council, to divide all the categories of goods that are made in Canada or conceivably might be made in Canada, and the conception need only be in the mind of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). It does not need to be in anyone else's mind. He never has to explain to anyone, no matter how arbitrary, no matter how unjust the decision. As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has pointed out one of his minions could make the decision without even the minister knowing about it. He decides that something or other is custom made to specifications.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: We do not have minions in the department under this minister.

The minister knows they are exactly the same people in the department, except for a few new recruits, as they were before. No one in this house has more respect for the civil servants than I have. The civil servants are there to do a certain job. The ministers are there to do another job, and parliament is here to do another job. Parliament never intended that a grade 4 clerk should decide what the Customs Tariff of this country should be or what duties people should pay. This, in fact, is what is going to happen under this legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Sheer nonsense.

The description of that statement as sheer nonsense does not make it nonsense. It merely indicates that the minister believes it is more effective to make an exclamation like that than to attempt to refute the argument.
This afternoon the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) used an argument that is always used by good tyrants when he said it would be more efficient for the Minister of National Revenue to make certain of these decisions
Customs Tariff
than for the tariff board to make them. It does not matter whether it is fair; it does not matter whether it is just; it does not matter whether this is an arbitrary tax imposed upon the people, it is more efficient. The other argument is that it could be done confidentially. In other words, the minister decides in secret on the basis of secret information whether the tax shall be low or high or no tax at all. This is precisely what we are doing over the whole range of goods that may or may not be made in Canada. We are going to let the minister decide and the minister will have the final decision in every case.
It is true that, on a certain limited range of facts, an appeal will be permitted if the minister decides the goods are shelf goods. All the minister needs to do is decide they are custom made, and that finishes it. The fact of the matter is that the minister is being given the very widest possible powers, powers that cannot be challenged anywhere except in the House of Commons. Then, of course, we will be told it is not in the public interest to produce this information. If the information is so secret that the tariff board cannot be trusted to receive it, I can imagine how likely this government is to give it to members- of the House of Commons.
The plain fact is that even supposing the government does want to change the definition of class or kind-there are a lot of objections to that but I do not propose to go into them because it seems to me that, Mr. Speaker, would be transgressing your ruling which I respect-because they are not satisfied that the courts have properly interpreted the law, some other course should have been followed. This all-wise Minister of Finance knows better than the courts. He knows better than the Speaker what the rules of the house should be. He alone has the key to the mind of the late Mr. Fielding. He has told us what Mr. Fielding meant when this legislation was enacted in 1907.
Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Oh, certainly.
Would he inform the house as to whether or not he holds opinions about legislation and expresses them in this house?

Oh, yes, I certainly do hold opinions. However, I have never, in this house, described the decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada as an erosion of the law. Perhaps that is because I am not an eminent barrister like the Minister of Finance. It does seem to me that is an odd way of describing the decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada. That has been done over and over again and was done again today by the minister.

The hon. gentleman knows so much more about it. How does he propose to get around it? I grant that parliament has a perfect right to change the law if we do not like the interpretation of the law by the Supreme Court of Canada. We are the legislators, but we are the legislators and not the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue sitting alone in his closet. That is the whole point. If this government were honest and straightforward-I do not mean honest in money matters, but I mean honest and straightforward in putting forward its legislation-
When you get the budget, you will talk about honesty in money matters.

The fact that it is bungling and cannot tell the difference between a deficit and surplus does not surprise me. We had an indication of that when hon. members of the government talked about the way in which this country was being overtaxed at a time when the debt was being paid off instead of being accumulated. We are aware of the fact that the minister does not understand these things. We know that very well. We realize that this country is burdened with the most incompetent Minister of Finance it has had within living memory.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: That statement is even more crazy than the other one.

I rise on a point of order. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has allowed himself to be diverted from the subject under discussion by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I think he has now gone completely beyond the subject under discussion.

I am always grateful to the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) who has helped me out more than once in the house. I am particularly grateful for the last time he did so. I will therefore come back to the point I was making and it was this. On March 31, 1958, the people of Canada did not decide that one or two ministers of the crown should be given the tariff making power. They decided to let the right hon. gentleman who is now the head of his government and his friends carry on the government of Canada; but they did so in large part, in my opinion, because they were told that this was a government that was going to restore the rights of parliament.
I personally confess that I was never impressed with the suggestion that parliament had ever lost any of its rights prior to that time, but I certainly know it has lost some of them since then. It certainly did so in that very summer of 1958. In that very summer of 1958 the first thing they did was to

do what they are trying to make a more thorough job of now, that is to say, to take away from this parliament the tariff making power and to put it in the hands of one single minister who will not be answerable in that regard even to the cabinet, whose decisions may not even be known,-
There is no obligation to publish.

-and who will be able to make one kind of decision in the case of one applicant and, when there is in fact a similar set of facts, make another kind of decision in the case of another applicant, with no power whatsoever on anyone's part to do anything.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Is the hon. member suggesting that such power should be given to the minister only if he has the advantage of a glass ball in order to communicate with the late Mr. Fielding?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

When we rose at six o'clock I was referring to the fact that one of the principal effects of this bill is to take away from parliament in any effective sense the right to make the tariff, the right to determine the duty which will be paid by a taxpayer with respect to a whole range of goods, while the government arrogates to itself the right to determine in a completely arbitrary fashion whether a particular article is custom made or shelf goods.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Was not the former done in 1904, and does the hon. gentleman object to that?

By "the former" I presume the hon. gentleman means that a decision was made by parliament in 1904 that if something was made in Canada-which is, of course, a matter of fact, not a matter of opinion-the duty would be a certain amount, while if something was not made in Canada the duty would be a different amount. That is something which is done by parliament. It is true
Customs Tariff
the determination of whether or not something was made or not made in Canada was arrived at by the administration. In the relatively simple industrial conditions of 1907 I do not think those determinations of fact would have required, in many cases, any very expert knowledge. If there is any defence for this bill at all it surely is that the whole distinction between shelf goods and custom made goods is something which no one would have thought of making in 1907. I do assert that if we are to say that in the case of the shelf goods they must actually be made in Canada but that in the case of custom made goods there must merely be a capacity for them to be made in Canada, then at least those questions should be determined publicly and in the open. Parliament should make definitions with regard to them, and then decisions should be reached publicly and in the open instead of secretly and in the minister's office without the right of appeal and in an utterly arbitrary manner.
That is the point which hon. members opposite are either utterly incapable of comprehending or, as I suspect, utterly unwilling to comprehend. The fact is that if the questions of whether goods are custom made or shelf goods is decided before a public tribunal where argument can be heard we could all see whether or not the will of parliament was being carried out. When those decisions are reached in secret, who is to decide? There is no reason why the minister should not say that the most ordinary thing made on an assembly line is a custom made article. That would not be an honest thing to do, but it would be within the power of the minister to do it. I contend that if we are going to make this distinction between custom made and shelf goods, then when a determination is made there should be proper publication of it and of all the reasons for it; there should be a determination before a tribunal and not in secret and in an arbitrary way by the minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman agree with the distinction in the first instance?

That is totally irrelevant to the amendment and to my argument. When I come to speak on the second reading I shall deal with that question. However, I am endeavouring at the present time to confine myself strictly to the amendment-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member seeks to avoid answering the question.

The hon. gentleman can go on muttering, but I suggest he listen. There are three ways in which I suggest the rights of parliament are being taken away. In the

Customs Tariff
first place the arbitrary and secret power to decide whether or not an article is custom made destroys any effective control by parliament over the tariff. In the second place, the arbitrary power to decide whether adequate facilities exist destroys any effective control by parliament or, indeed, anyone else except the minister himself, and, third, the question of what is a reasonable period of time, which is also left to the arbitrary opinion of the minister or one of his officials, also, I suggest, involves an encroachment on the rights of parliament.
Many hon. members will have read in the local newspapers the brief accounts of the budget speech made today by the chancellor of the exchequer in the United Kingdom. They will have seen that the chancellor has asked that he be given the power to raise or lower certain duties there by not more than 10 per cent to meet certain economic problems which may arise in the course of the next year, and that he has also asked to have that power limited strictly to a term ending on August 31, 1962 unless at a subsequent session of parliament it should be renewed. This is precisely the difference between what is and what is not disruptive of parliamentary control. Here, the government of the United Kingdom is seeking, as all governments must at times, certain limited powers to act quickly. But those powers are carefully and clearly defined and a time limit is placed upon them. It will not be beyond the recollection of many hon. gentlemen sitting on the treasury benches how much importance they attached not so many years ago to the matter of a time limit in connection with powers given to the governor in council. I contend that clause 3 of this bill justifies my saying that the power of parliament effectively to determine the tariff is being taken away from parliament.
I said I would deal with one argument which has been advanced from the government benches and I think there is no better way of dealing with the argument raised by the Minister of Finance than to repeat a quotation given a few days ago in this house by my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River. If you think, Mr. Speaker, that I am quoting from another debate, then I am, sir, but what I am quoting is from a debate which took place in another session. I am quoting what the Prime Minister said when he was on this side of the house in 1950 and the words could not be more apt than they are:
The attitude that an opposition is something to put up with on occasion is prevalent in some quarters... If the cabinet is to be trusted-
And we are being asked here to trust, not the cabinet, but one minister only-
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
-and if we are to accept at face value what ministers say, we had better all be absent from this house.
That is really what we are talking about. We are saying that if the taxing power, the determination of the rights of taxation, and the mode of taxation are to be taken away from this house and vested in one minister of the crown without appeal and without publicity, in secret, then indeed we had better not be here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That was done by Laurier and Fielding.
Get up and tell us about it.

Mr. Speaker, I must say a few words on this amendment before the vote is put. It is a very strange amendment coming from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who was a member of a government which, time after time, brought in the type of legislation about which he is now complaining. I do not know what particular passage he was quoting from a few minutes ago in using the words of the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) but undoubtedly it was something very similar to the proposal now before us.
I have to admit that the words of subclause 3 of clause 2(a) have troubled me since I first read them, because undue delegation of authority to the executive and the removal of the right of appeal are two principles to which I am opposed. Under the previous government they were used constantly until they almost became commonplace. So far as I know this is the first piece of legislation that this government has introduced in nearly four years in office which contains a provision of this type, in which the minister's decision is final. I feel, therefore, that we have to look at this clause very carefully before passing judgment on it.
Quite a number of matters in this bill will require interpretation. I would like to list them as they appear to me and then examine which of these provisions will require the interpretation of the minister and which of them will require the interpretation of the courts. The first provision that will have to be decided is, what are goods other than goods custom made? The second matter is, how shall the word "approximately" be applied to a given situation? The third is, what is the definition of the words "class or kind"? The fourth is, what is the definition of the words "made or produced in Canada"? The fifth matter is, do adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic

production of such goods, within a reasonable period of time? The sixth matter involves the interpretation of subclause 2 of the legislation. The seventh matter is, [DOT]yvhat is the normal Canadian consumption, and the final matter involves an interpretation of subsection 9 of section 6 of the act, as amended by this bill.
I have set forth eight matters in which, it seems to me, a decision must be arrived at for the administration of the bill. Of these eight matters, three are commended to the decision of the minister, and five are left to the courts' interpretation. I realize that we cannot make a decision in respect of the balance of probabilities or because of majority alone. I do want to point out that this is not a case where the act is passed and committed thereupon immediately to the sole discretion of the minister. In certain matters his discretion is final, but in the majority of matters that is not so.
Furthermore, this is an isolated piece of legislation designed to meet a particular need and does not indicate, in my belief, any trend. The minister has carefully and adequately explained the special circumstances under which the three items are committed to the sole decision of the Minister of National Revenue. I accept that explanation and feel that in this particular instance it is sufficient. I must say, however, that if such a trend were to appear in the legislation introduced by this government, or any government, it would cause one to be concerned and, if such legislation became commonplace, I would have to take a much stronger stand. However, I am not going to stand out in the lobby when the vote is taken on this amendment. I am going to vote against it because I do not feel that a sufficient case has been made out against the legislation introduced by the minister.
Hon. members opposite may say I am in an anomalous position in that I am speaking generalities in one case and specifics in another. I would like to point out to them that this is the very situation they are in. They have been talking today in grandiose terms against protective tariffs in generalities. They say they are against protective tariffs and against this type of legislation in general terms but when we come to specific items such as automobiles, textiles, fruit and vegetables and plywood, time and again hon. members in the opposition have risen to ask what the government intends to do to protect these industries. When the government makes some announcement of a policy to assist these various industries, and there have been several such announcements, opposition members are particularly in accord.

I mentioned particularly the fruit and vegetable industry, and I would suggest that if it were not for certain protection given to the fruit farmers they would in certain parts of British Columbia and Ontario have had a very difficult year. I point out these matters because, as a matter of interest, it is easy for an individual to say in general that he is against something but when dealing with specifics the same individuals are for them. (Translation ):

Mr. Speaker, this bill is designed to amend sections 2 to 6 of the Customs Tariff with regard to goods of a class or kind made in Canada.
If we look closely at it we note that it is unquestionably a bill that will lead directly to protectionist measures.
I refer the house in particular to subsection (3) of section 2A. It is clearly stated there that the minister's decision will be final.
Therefore, I suggest that the purpose of this bill is to abolish the essential rights of parliament, as well as the powers of the tariff board, and to confer absolute and arbitrary power upon the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan).
I read the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) at the resolution stage. This is what he said then:
This measure will ensure a greater discretion to the Minister of National Revenue with regard to decisions to be made under section 3.
It is not a matter of greater discretion but of an absolute and irrevocable power. It is nothing less than a reactionary right.
In other words, taxpayers are being deprived of a right recognized by British law and by tradition.
Regarding the dangers of using this discretionary power, I wish to read a few sentences from a book entitled:
(Text):
"Senate special committee on taxation, 1945."
I am referring to a brief presented by the

Customs Tariff
income tax payers' association to the Senate committee in 1945. This brief was read by Professor McDougall, associate professor of commerce, Queen's University. Here is what the brief had to say concerning this precise problem of ministerial discretion, at page 297:
May we recall in this connection the famous saying of the Middlesex rebels, "Where discretion begins, law, liberty and safety end."
In this brief the question is asked, "How is discretion exercised?" The question is answered in the brief in this way:
Normally it is given to the minister. In practice it is in the hands of the deputy minister and through him it is frequently exercised by other officials including junior assessors. Junior assessors first deal with and report on income tax returns. These reports go to head office and are there either confirmed or overruled by more senior officials. It is reasonable to believe that only the more important or "larger" matters ever reach the desk of even the deputy minister-and perhaps never the minister. The fact is, therefore, that ministerial discretion is exercised, never by the minister, in a few instances by the deputy minister but in the main by various clerks, assessors, other officials of the income tax service. One can well realize that the only safe decision for assessors and clerks to make is against the taxpayer.
Then, at page 299 we find the following:
We strongly urge therefore that the taxing power be returned to parliament where it belongs and that ministerial discretion be limited to administrative acts only, such as the prescribing of forms, the specifying of dates for filing and similar powers which pertain rightfully to the minister's duties as an administrator. In cases where it appears that it is impossible to avoid the granting of some judicial or semi-judicial functions to the minister or his officials, the exercise of discretion by them should never be final but should be subject to appeal to an independent appeal tribunal in the manner hereinafter referred to in respect of appeals.
(Translation):
Now, Mr. Speaker, the tradition is that parliament enacts legislation and that judicial or semi-judicial bodies are responsible for its interpretation. Such is the custom and tradition.
With this Bill C-72, we are taking a step backward. I say it is unwise to get away from this tradition. No serious reason has been advanced so far to justify such unappealable decisions as are provided for under this bill.
As the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) rightly mentioned, a customs duty is a tax, and the taxing power belongs exclusively to the House of Commons.
The immediate result of this bill will be to evoke feelings of uneasiness and uncertainty in Canadian business circles, because in many cases, very costly goods and considerable amounts will be involved.
Following the fears expressed by the members of the opposition in the debate on the resolution, I would have hoped that the minister would reconsider; apparently, he has done

no such thing, or if he has, he has persisted in his initial attitude.
If this bill is passed, it can only be a cause for regret, because some of its provisions are contrary to the traditions and essential rules of parliament.
The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), in his amendment, proposes, for the above reasons, that the bill be not now read a second time.
In closing, may I add this. It is rather strange to find that the very people who opposed the amendment put forward before six o'clock by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River are those who, in the past three or four years, have been so vociferous in calling for the maintenance of parliamentary rights and those century old rights which we have acquired through parliamentary tradition.
(Text):

Mr. Speaker, as a member from British Columbia, a province whose welfare depends greatly on export industries, I cannot subscribe to anything or any trend which may adversely affect the welfare of those industries or increase the capital cost of the plants and operations which produce those goods. In this I may be classed by many as provincially minded but I do not consider myself so. I sincerely believe I am thinking in the best interests of all of Canada. Furthermore, as a citizen of British Columbia, a province in which discretionary powers of ministers have not always been used in what I consider to be the best interests of the people, I oppose granting such powers to ministers of the crown excepting in circumstances of extreme necessity and urgency. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to support this amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the house ready for the question?

Mr. Speaker, I will vote for this amendment because the bill proposes to remove from parliament certain of its taxing powers. I believe this is the first time I have seen this happen in the house. I recall vividly the debate on the Emergency Powers Act which was to apply for a limited period of time. I recall the minister and other members of the treasury benches found fault with the government at that time because they said the government was assuming powers that rightfully belonged to parliament. At that time the emergency powers bill had a time limit. The bill now before us has no time limit. It will be passed by a big majority in the house and can only be revoked by a majority of the house.

This afternoon the minister referred to the fact that certain measures would be taken because of confidential information. This suggests to me that because certain information would be confidential the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) could not be compelled to give any information to the house concerning why certain duties had been applied. As members of the house we are surrendering our right to tax and also our right to obtain information as to the reasons why certain duties are imposed. If there has been erosion by the tariff board, if there has been erosion by the Supreme Court of Canada, if there has been contraction in the meaning of the words "class or kind", I would much prefer to see the government spell out the remedy in legislation and leave the right of appeal to the tariff board and to the Exchequer Court of Canada.
I think this legislation could lead to abuses. I am not referring to the present Minister of National Revenue any more than to his successors. To all intents and purposes this legislation will become permanent and will be removed only because of abuses or other causes. When the minister replies I would ask him to explain why this particular aspect of taxation cannot be spelled out in legislation as is the case with all other forms of taxation. In other words, is it not possible to bring forward a broader definition of "class or kind" goods which will stick so far as the tariff board and the Exchequer Court of Canada are concerned?
This afternoon the minister said, I think, that the Minister of National Revenue would have the final decision on three points. The first was with respect to whether goods are shelf goods or custom made to specification. It strikes me that these two things can be defined in such a way as to distinguish them. Second, in the case of shelf goods he said that the Minister of National Revenue would have the power to decide whether or not Canadian production amounted to 10 per cent of our consumption. This is factual information which should be available to all and I do not think such a matter should come before the minister for decision. I can see that there might be some difficulty with respect to the third point, namely, whether in the case of custom made goods adequate facilities exist in Canada to make them economically within a reasonable period of time.
So far as the first two points are concerned, I think the government could spell them out in legislation. In the one case factual information is involved and in the other case it is just a matter of a definition to distinguish shelf goods and custom made goods. I do not think that would be very difficult. The only difficulty that might arise,
