Customs Tariff
and which I think all of us appreciate, is whether or not facilities exist in Canada for the production of the custom goods made to specifications.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks at this time will be rather brief. I listened with particular interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who seemed to be especially concerned about the loss of the rights of parliament in connection with the application of tariffs and duties. I should like to remind him that perhaps one of the last acts of the former government of which he was a minister was to impose a fair value for duty purposes on fruits and vegetables. They took this action and raised the tariff on certain fruits at that time, which was indeed a raising of tariffs without consulting parliament.
I remember the announcement in the newspapers at that time with respect to this action of the cabinet by order in council. It was pointed out in press reports that the then minister of finance, Walter Harris, had seen fit to take this action. He had reached into the closet and pulled out an old act passed in the days of the Bennett regime which had not been used for 22 years. However, when the chips were down and the former government was in trouble it decided to put the act into effect. This is indeed quite contrary to the opinion expressed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate at this time. What was good at that time surely should be good at the present time.
Last year or the year before the matter of fair value for duty purposes was debated in this house and discretionary powers were placed in the hands of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) to take action if he saw fit. We went through the whole matter at that time. It was said that in taking such action we were only looking for retaliation from the United States but there has not been any retaliation, and after listening to all the debate I still feel that to place this reclassification matter in the hands of the Minister of National Revenue is to place it where it should be.
Perhaps the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) would prefer to have the present regulations continue whereby in order to secure a reclassification the matter has to go to the tariff board. Sometimes the board takes a year or two years to make a recommendation and then the matter has to come before parliament which may take six months or more to dispose of it. Therefore I think it is quite in order that we should cut out a lot of this red tape and get down to placing the responsibilities where they belong.

Division
I did not hear all the remarks of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson) but when I came into the house he was referring to statements I had made at the resolution stage. I think the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River will understand that I respect the opinions he expresses in the house on many occasions, though I do not always agree with him. I should like to say that when I spoke on the resolution stage I was speaking more or less in general terms. At that time I referred to several commodities that could be made in Canada, some of which in fact are made here, and the fact that goods of a similar kind came into this country duty free. While the bill might not cover all the commodities I mentioned, I felt it was a step in the right direction and I still feel that way. I know that the house is anxious to get along with the bill, Mr. Speaker, and I believe these are the only points I wish to make. My only disappointment with respect to the bill is that it perhaps does not go far enough.

I said earlier when I was making a few observations on the amendment put forward by my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River that I intended to abide by the ruling of His Honour the Deputy Speaker and speak strictly on the amendment, reserving the general observations which I had to make about the bill untill we came to discuss the minister's motion for second reading.
I may say that it does seem to me that extraordinary as it was for the government to introduce this legislation at any time, in the light of what has happened in the weeks, the months, since this legislation was first proposed in the budget speech on December 20, during most of which time the minister has postponed it from time to time so that there would not be an opportunity to debate it consecutively-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is utterly without truth.

While the minister has been flitting back and forth to British Columbia in equally futile efforts, during that time we have seen in every other country of commercial importance in the free world increasing indication that the whole trend, except in our own country, is toward the liberation of trade not toward the restriction of trade. Yet here are we under the present government going against the stream of freedom in the world at the present time.

It seems to me that anyone who has paid any attention to what was said as recently as last week by the British Prime Minister when he was here would appreciate how ill-timed, how unfortunate it is for the real interest of the country to be moving in the direction in which we are moving at the present time. It has already been made clear -and I do not intend to traverse this ground again this evening-that all the great export industries of this country, the industries which are finding competition increasingly difficult to meet as other countries rehabilitate their industry and build up their capital, are really greatly concerned about this move by the government which, they fear, as my hon. friend from Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) pointed out at an earlier stage in the debate, will have the effect of increasing their costs or alternatively, driving them into the use of less efficient machinery or more costly machinery than would otherwise be the case.
It seems to me that these broad considerations ought to have influenced the government. It seems they should have taken account of the reaction in the world at large and the reaction of our export industries on whose success the income of about one of every four Canadians depends. It seems to me the government should have been warned by all this that we were moving in the wrong direction and that they should call a halt and abandon this legislation.
The Minister of Finance has told us over and over again that the principal reason for bringing this legislation before parliament at this time is that over the years the tariff board and the courts have eroded the law. In other words, the minister has said that neither the tariff board nor the courts knew what parliament meant and that the effect of the law as it was until 1949 has been changed by the decisions of the board and of the courts. I must say this is the first time in my recollection that a minister of the crown who is also an eminent member of the bar has criticized in this fashion decisions of the courts including the highest court of our country. However, as I said earlier, if the government feels the law as it now stands and as it has been interpreted by the courts does not represent what the majority of the members of this parliament want, then I suggest they should change the law and not attempt to abolish the rule of law.
Even if the supreme court has been as misguided as the Minister of Finance represented it as having been, the hon. gentleman is surely in error in suggesting that we must extinguish the jurisdiction of the court in the future. That, of course, will be the effect of this legislation.
Customs Tariff
In response to a request which I made at an earlier stage of the proceedings in committee-a request that we should be furnished with concrete examples of this alleged erosion; erosion which I may say the minister repeatedly said had taken place between 1950 and 1960-the hon. gentleman went back and spent some time discussing two or three cases in 1933 and 1934 which could not have had any conceivable relevance to the matter before us nor even to the proposition he himself had made. Then the hon. gentleman went on to cite the case in 1950 of the .22 rifles. This was the only case he took the trouble to discuss in some detail, and the minister was not very explicit even about that. But to the extent that he was explicit he was quite wrong.
What actually happened in 1950 was that the tariff board did not uphold the decision of the deputy minister at that time but, instead, went back to a decision of the deputy minister in 1939 and supported it. So, far from there being any erosion by the tariff board there would appear to have been some misinterpretation in 1950 of the meaning, as it was understood in 1939 of this legislation by parliament, and the tariff board, as one would expect, went back to that earlier decision.
The Minister of Finance, with the vast experience that he acquired over the years in opposition and the very brief experience he has had as Minister of Finance, in which his capacity for sound judgment in respect of financial problems has been demonstrated in such striking fashion to the country and to the house, has made a suggestion that is difficult to accept. The tariff board which, during practically all this period, he said, was characterized by this erosion, was presided over by Mr. Hector McKinnon who perhaps more than any other person in this country was in the confidence of the ministers of finance who were responsible for the law as it was in 1939, and in 1930 when Mr. Dunning first proposed this legislation in its modern form. To suggest that Mr. Hector McKinnon, who made these decisions, did not know what the law meant, but that the Minister of Finance who was opposed to the government that was responsible both for proposing and administering of the law is endowed with some special insight into it, is a proposal which every informed person will find very hard to swallow.
As my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) has pointed out, Mr. McKinnon, after being for many years the principal tariff adviser to the Minister of Finance, and for 15 years the chairman of the tariff board, and even more extraordinary, after this vote of want of confidence by the Minister of Finance in

Customs Tariff
Mr. McKinnon, he is still employed now, after his retirement, to advise the government and to conduct negotiations on its behalf. It does seem to me that the government would have been wise to think up some different excuse for this legislation than an attack upon Mr. McKinnon's knowledge of the law and on the capacity of the Supreme Court of Canada to interpret it. The Minister of Finance having misrepresented the rifle case to the house, then referred us to a lot of other cases but did not make the slightest attempt to show in any respect whatsoever how there could have been erosion.
That will take some days to look up.

The most serious of all the objections, except the one the house has already expressed a view on, but which is equal to it in its import, is the deliberate attempt of the government to abolish the rule of law, a deliberate attempt on the part of the government to exclude the taxpayer from the court, to which, up to now, he has had access.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. gentleman would agree with me that the question has been disposed of on the amendment?

No, sir, I do not think that question has been disposed of by the amendment. The amendment we had before us dealt with the taking away from parliament the tariff making powers, but did not in any way deal with the question of the denial of the right of appeal. It may be that-in order to show that the rights of parliament were taken away; there was, incidentally, reference to this other matter, but it does not seem to me that it was in any sense whasoever the subject of the amendment-this denial of the right of appeal, which is clearly set out in the legislation itself, and which is one of the fundamental terms of the legislation which the government has argued is necessary in order to make the legislation effective, is every bit as objectionable as the attempt to take from parliament its power to determine tariffs.
At page 1668 of Hansard of February 2, 1961 while in committee, the Minister of Finance in a reply to an intervention of mine, had the following to say:
-He is denying the right to an appeal in the future, and that is what we are objecting to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You see, Mr. Chairman, this speech has been introduced under the guise of asking a question.
Well, answer it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Answer the speech? I shall be prepared to answer anything that is raised in the committee and I shall be prepared to answer this point, hut I will first draw to your attention, Mr. Chairman, the manner in which the

hon. member, having taken to himself the right to ask a question, then comes forward in typical style to supply his own answer, which is a most erroneous and misleading answer, and then sits down with a look of utter satisfaction although the answer he has supplied to his own question is wrong.
You give the answer, then.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I make my own statement?

Give the answer; never mind all the verbiage.
The minister then went off on some other theme. He has obviously been exceedingly uncomfortable about this matter and has sought, as far as possible, to evade direct answers. There is no way of getting around the fact that on three of the most important questions of fact-indeed one of them is absolutely fundamental-the minister's decision is to be final and not subject to appeal. I do not think that is in question. I have a good many references and am prepared to read them if it is. The minister decides finally on the basis of confidential information, without review or appeal of any kind, even by the cabinet, what goods are shelf goods and what custom made goods. This is a question of fact in respect of which it has never been necessary in the past to have a determination by the tariff board or the courts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman going to answer the question I asked in regard to this point?
Perhaps the hon. member would like to repeat it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The question I asked the hon. gentleman earlier, which he avoided, was whether he approved of the distinction that was made between shelf goods and custom goods made to specification?

I certainly do not approve of the distinction in the form it is made in this bill. I do not approve of giving the Minister of National Revenue the power to determine whether an article is custom made or shelf goods. As to the broader question which the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) has asked-it is a very important one-I would say this. I have the very gravest doubts as to whether, under the obligations we entered into in the Canada-United States trade agreement, and subsequently in GATT, that it is a proper thing to do; I fear it is a thing that will be regarded as an infringement of obligations solemnly entered into for this parliament to say that goods are made in Canada, and to use that provision of the law, in respect of things that are not made in Canada.

That is made perfectly clear with the definition that is given here of "custom made to specifications", and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada to make them. I am sure that, if I were the representative of another country having commercial relations with Canada, another country which had agreed to the provisions that now exist in the law, I would regard this as an evasion of that law. I am perfectly sure that if the Americans undertook to do anything similar we would, as the minister used to say when he was over here, talk to them in no uncertain terms. Well, he does not talk that loud any more now when he has to go down to Washington and see them. In fact, what began with a bang is ending in a whimper so far as the minister is concerned when he goes to Washington.
But the plain fact is if the Americans made a similar distinction in relation to something that we thought they had conceded to us in a trade agreement there would be a mighty howl in Canada about it, and every Canadian who is honest with himself knows it. To me it looks like pretty sharp practice. But I say, sir, that if any distinction is to be made it should be made clearly and explicitly by this parliament, and that the question of fact should be determinable by the tariff board as other questions have been determinable by the tariff board in the past in respect of these "made in Canada" rules. In the past every aspect of the facts has been open to review by the tariff board. Now certain aspects are taken away from them. This is the whole point.
There might be an argument for saying that there should be no court of appeal, no review instituted on something which has never been reviewed in the past, administrative decisions which have never been the subject of appeal in the past. But here, sir, we are deliberately saying that some of the facts which in the past have been appealable to the tariff board and to the courts are no longer to be appealable. In other words, we are extinguishing an existing right to judicial determination of facts and vesting the decision instead in a single minister. It seems to me, sir, that that is far and away the most serious aspect of this legislation apart, as I have said, from the derogation of the rights of parliament which we believe the bill also embodies.
The most serious feature is, of course, the minister making the final decision. I ask the minister again why? I ask the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), who has some regard for these matters, why should the tariff board not be able to look at all these facts? Surely the question of whether an article is custom made or shelf goods is a
Customs Tariff
question of fact which could be determined in the open, publicly, with argument heard on both sides.
One of the ministers said that it was a very simple matter; the other rather suggested it was not; we have had a good deal of double talk of that sort. To me it should be a matter of fact, and it should be determined in the open and publicly.
This is not a small matter; this is a matter that can affect business operations and affect employment. I understand that at the beginning of the afternoon, before I was able to get into the house, the minister talked about this so-called erosion having affected employment adversely. Well, we are very much afraid that these arbitrary decisions, against which there is going to be no appeal, are going to affect employment adversely.
Then, sir, why should normal Canadian consumption of shelf goods be abstracted from the list of facts which the tariff board can determine? Even when something is ruled to be shelf goods, why should just one of the facts be taken away? I cannot give any rational explanation of that at all and I have not heard any from the other side of the house. The tariff board can determine the production but not the consumption. If anything might have been considered secret, one would have thought that the production would be more apt to be something about which producers would be concerned with maintaining secrecy. Surely the total consumption in Canada should not be a matter of secrecy. The suggestion that there is some mysterious statistic available to the Minister of National Revenue that would not be available to the tariff board is a suggestion that anybody with the faintest experience with administration knows is too ridiculous an argument to be seriously accepted for a moment.
It seems to me, sir, that there is just no rational justification whatsoever for this clause. The result is that the denial of the right of appeal has created in many minds the impression the government is doing this deliberately because it wants to have the capacity to favour some people as opposed to others. I am not making this charge myself. This is an impression that is widespread in the country and it is the kind of impression that is bound to be created whenever these secret and arbitrary powers are given to ministers of the crown.
Why do they want them to be secret? Why do they want them to be arbitrary? What are they afraid of? I remember Mr. Graydon, the former leader of the opposition, would talk about pulling up the blinds and letting in

Customs Tariff"
the light. The Prime Minister used to be very eloquent on this subject when he was on this side of the house.
As I say, even if the government does want to change these definitions, even if it does want the rest of this legislation, it is impossible to see why it feels it necessary to deny and to nullify the right of appeal that now exists.
I reminded the committee at an earlier stage, and I should like to recall it once more of a statement made by the Minister of Finance some years ago, which I think all of us in this house should ponder. I may say I do not too often agree with the Minister of Finance. He was not minister of finance then, but I certainly agree with what he said at that time. This is what he said, and it is very apt. It applies with great force to the legislation now before us. On June 7, 1955, the Minister of Finance said, as recorded at page 4524 of Hansard of that day:
Sir, hon. members, as I conceive it, were elected to this house to legislate, not to abdicate the legislative function to the government. They are elected to preserve freedom, not to open the doors or admit the Trojan horse of executive power into the citadel of Canadian freedom.
We of Her Majesty's loyal opposition have fought this kind of legislation, and I think we can point to some success.
Well, considering the kind of government we have now, I am not sure, sir, that we will be able to point to any success; but I do say that that is no reason why we should not fight this attempt to abrogate the rule of law, this attempt to take away access to the courts which now exists, this attempt by a government that only a year ago asked this parliament, and got this parliament unanimously to enact a bill of rights, to take away one of the fundamental rights that bill was supposed to safeguard. That, sir, is in the highest degree astonishing to us on this side of the house and, of course, not only to us.
I should like to refer to, and to express as my own views, views that were expressed on March 18 in a journal published in this country which is not a notorious proponent of free trade, a journal which I think may fairly be regarded as a supporter of, at any rate, moderate protection. I refer to the Financial Post. As I say, I make these words completely my own. That paper said:
For all Canadians, as well as for manufacturers and importers, a very basic principle is at stake in the current revision of the Canadian Customs Tariff Act. It is the right of a private citizen to appeal to an independent tribunal if he believes he has been wronged by those empowered to administer and put into effect government legislation. This is precisely the right that is being taken away in one part of the government bill, currently before the house, to define whether goods are of a "class or kind" made in Canada. In three specific matters, the decision of the Minister of National Revenue

will be final and, if the bill passes in its present form, there can be no appeal to the independent tariff board. This is unwanted, unnecessary and dangerous. The thing should be strangled in its cradle.
Indeed, sir, one wonders why it was ever born, especially with the paternity of the right hon. gentleman who also sponsored the bill of rights. Therefore, sir, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this house declines to proceed with a bill the fundamental terms of which, by seeking to deny an appeal by the subject to the courts now provided by law, are repugnant to the spirit and objectives of the Canadian bill of rights."

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before I place this amendment before the house, is there any comment?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I declare the amendment lost.
Because of the lateness of the hour, Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I might be permitted to move the adjournment of the debate.
No.

If hon. members object, I shall begin. We have been entertained over a considerable number of days at various stages of this measure by spokesmen for the Liberal party. I can remember very well an election campaign in 1940 when the speaker so adequately and so graphically explained to his audience that, despite the differences or the professed differences of the Liberals and Conservatives on this matter of tariffs, to the consumers and to the producers of Canada each time there was a change of government all it meant was higher tariffs regardless of any election promises or any speeches they had made in years gone by.
I also thought that the Liberals had a great deal of gall to be appealing to the parliament of Canada and to the people of Canada at
Business of the House
this stage with regard to the rights of parliament. After all, I do not think I am the only one in Canada who has a bit of a memory. We can remember only too well that a limited number of years ago the Liberal party of Canada showed no concern for the rights of parliament.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member will agree with me that the issue with regard to parliament delegating its authority was disposed of by the first amendment. The second amendment disposed of another question. The hon. member has a rather limited scope now in the debate on second reading.

I should like to express my disappointment. The minister today made it abundantly clear that he was not happy with the decisions of the tariff board. He spoke of erosion of the customs tariff legislation that had occurred because of the decisions of the tariff board. To me the minister came very close to expressing contempt for what is in effect a court of law established by this parliament.
I wonder whether I might move the adjournment of the debate, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will call it ten o'clock.
